---
title: "Pass Protection: Slides, Man Schemes, and Who Blocks the Extra Guy"
subtitle: "Five linemen, a clock, and a defense that decides after the snap how many are coming: how an offense keeps its quarterback upright, and how to see it from the couch"
description: "Pass protection from the ground up: why protection is counting, the pocket and the launch point, slide and man (big-on-big) protection, the half-slide, Mike identification, the back's and tight end's jobs (check-release, chip), max protect, scat and empty protections, hot routes and sight adjustments when rushers outnumber blockers, the tackle's kick slide and his vertical and jump sets, punch and anchor, passing off stunts (switch or stay), and the numbers that measure it all: pressure, hits and hurries, pressure rate, time to throw and sack rate."
glossary:
  "Slide protection": "A pass protection in which the offensive linemen block areas instead of men: each slides one way and takes the gap on that side, whoever rushes through it, while a back or tight end takes the edge rusher the slide leaves behind."
  "Man protection": {def: "A pass protection in which each blocker is assigned a specific defender before the snap: usually the five linemen take the four defensive linemen and one linebacker, and the running back takes the next linebacker.", aliases: ["BOB", "Big-on-big"]}
  "Half-slide": "The NFL's most common six-man protection: the center and the two linemen on one side slide that way and block gaps, the two linemen on the other side block the man in front of them, and the running back takes the first extra rusher on the man side."
  "Max protect": "A protection that keeps seven or eight blockers in to block whatever the defense does (the five linemen plus tight ends and backs, with no check-releases), leaving only two or three receivers in the pattern, usually to buy time for a deep throw."
  "Scat protection": "A protection in which the running back lines up in the backfield but releases into his route at once instead of checking a blitzer first, so the line blocks and the quarterback is responsible for any extra rusher; the exact meaning of the word varies by playbook."
  "Empty protection (five-man)": "Pass protection with no back or tight end blocking, just the five linemen, as when the offense lines up with an empty backfield; if a sixth defender rushes, the quarterback must get rid of the ball before he arrives."
  Chip: "A quick hit by a tight end or back on a pass rusher, usually an edge rusher, to slow him down and help the tackle, delivered on the way out into a pass route; a back chips only after checking that no blitzer is his (check, chip, release)."
  "Check-release": "A back's or tight end's pass-protection rule: watch an assigned defender at the snap; if he rushes, block him; if he does not, release into a pass route."
  "Hot route": "A throw built into the play to beat an extra rusher: when the defense sends more rushers than the protection can block, the quarterback throws at once to a receiver running into the area the rusher just left. (In Madden the term means a pre-snap route change, which is something else.)"
  "Sight adjust": "A receiver changing his route after the snap because he sees a blitz, typically cutting a deep route off short so the quarterback, who sees the same blitz, can throw it quickly."
  "Free rusher": "A pass rusher nobody is assigned to block, either because the defense sent more rushers than the protection had blockers or because the blockers made a mistake."
  "Mike identification": {def: "The pre-snap call, made by the center or quarterback, that names one defender as the 'Mike' for this play; every blocker counts his assignment from that man, so all of them block the same picture.", aliases: ["MIKE ID"]}
  Pocket: "The protected space the blockers form around the quarterback on a pass: a cup with the interior linemen holding firm in front and the tackles giving ground on the sides."
  "Launch point": "The spot where the quarterback sets his feet to throw at the end of his drop; linemen set their depth to it so rushers are kept away from that exact spot."
  "Kick slide": "An offensive tackle's pass-set footwork: the outside foot kicks back and out, the inside foot slides after it, feet never crossing, so he moves backward and sideways while staying square to the rusher."
  "Vertical set": "A tackle's pass set straight back for depth, giving ground fast so a speed rusher has to run a longer arc around him."
  "Jump set": "An aggressive pass set in which a lineman moves forward or flat to meet the rusher at or near the line, taking away his running start; used most with quick throws."
  Punch: "A pass blocker's short, two-handed strike into the rusher's chest, inside his frame, to stop his momentum and win control of his body."
  Anchor: "A pass blocker's ability to stop being pushed backward by a power rush: hips down, base wide, feet regained, so the pocket does not collapse into the quarterback."
  "Pass-off (switch vs stay)": "How two adjacent blockers handle a stunt. Switch: each keeps his area and takes whoever comes into it, handing the first rusher to his neighbor. Stay: each follows the man he started on, wherever he goes."
  Pressure: "A pass rusher forcing the quarterback to change what he wanted to do: a sack, a hit, or a hurry. Definitions differ by data provider."
  "QB hit / hurry": "Two kinds of pressure short of a sack. A hit is contact that knocks the quarterback down or hits him as he throws; a hurry forces him to throw early or move off his spot without being hit."
  "Time to throw": "Seconds from the snap to the release of a pass; Next Gen Stats averages it over attempts, with sacks excluded."
  "Pressure rate": "Pressures divided by dropbacks: the share of pass plays on which the quarterback was pressured. A more stable measure of protection (or pass rush) than sacks."
---

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
#| output: false
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Polygon, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, defense, style
import gridiron.play as _gp

# Slightly smaller player markers than the book default: linemen stand about a yard and a half
# apart, and this chapter's diagrams are mostly about the space between them.
_gp.draw_marker.__defaults__ = (None, 0.62)

GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]   # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
RED = style.SERIES[7]
OL_KEYS = ["LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"]
SPLIT = 1.6                # center-to-guard and guard-to-tackle spacing, as in the rest of the book


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=None):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label or key)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line():
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled so the reader can follow each one."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, (i - 2) * SPLIT, k) for i, k in enumerate(OL_KEYS)]


def gun(rb_w=-1.5, qb_d=-5.0):
    """Shotgun quarterback with the back beside him (rb_w=None: no back)."""
    out = [O("QB", "QB", qb_d, 0.0, "Q")]
    if rb_w is not None:
        out.append(O("RB", "RB", qb_d, rb_w, "R"))
    return out


def four_down(mike=(4.5, 1.2), will=(4.5, -2.2), lbs=True):
    """A generic four-man front: ends outside the tackles, a 1-technique shaded on the center's
    left shoulder and a 3-technique on the right guard's outside shoulder, two linebackers."""
    out = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"),
           D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E")]
    if lbs:
        out += [D("MIKE", "MIKE", mike[0], mike[1], "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", will[0], will[1], "W")]
    return out


def to(p, key, end, kind="block", via=(), delay=0.0, speed=None):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end` as a block, rush, path, route or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, pts, frame="field", delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def timed(p, key, way, kind="path"):
    """Script a player for the frame strips: `way` = [(t, d, w), ...] absolute spots reached at time t
    (seconds after the snap). Standing still between two times is allowed."""
    cur = np.array(p._cur(key), dtype=float)
    tc, wait = 0.0, 0.0
    for t, d, w in way:
        nxt = np.array([d, w], dtype=float)
        dist = float(np.hypot(*(nxt - cur)))
        if dist < 1e-3:
            wait += t - tc
        else:
            p._add(kind, key, [tuple(cur), tuple(nxt)], speed=dist / (t - tc - 0.0), delay=wait)
            wait = 0.0
            cur = nxt
        tc = t
    return p


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.2, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.0, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def assign(fld, p, a, b, color=GREEN, lw=1.1, via=()):
    """A thin dotted 'this is my man' line from blocker `a` to defender `b` (alignment spots), optionally
    bent through absolute (d, w) points `via` so it does not run through another player."""
    pa, pb = p.players[a], p.players[b]
    pts = [(pa.d, pa.w), *via, (pb.d, pb.w)]
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (1, 1.6)), zorder=3.2)


def gap_oval(fld, p, w, d=0.15, width=1.25, height=1.0, color=GREEN, alpha=0.22):
    """Shade a gap on the line at width w: the area a sliding lineman owns."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), width, height, fc=color, alpha=alpha, ec=color, lw=0.9,
                             ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=1.6))


def tag(fld, p, key, text, dd=1.05, dw=0.0, color=GREEN, fontsize=7.4):
    """A small numbered tag just upfield of a player: the protection's count."""
    q = p.players[key]
    x, y = _P(fld, p, q.d + dd, q.w + dw)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color="white", ha="center", va="center", zorder=13,
                fontweight="bold", bbox=dict(boxstyle="circle,pad=0.16", fc=color, ec="none"))


def free_path(fld, p, pts, color=RED, lw=2.2, label=None, label_at=None):
    """A highlighted dashed path through absolute (d, w) points (a free rusher)."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=(0, (3, 1.8)), zorder=6)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=12,
                                     color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    if label:
        say(fld, p, *(label_at or pts[-1]), label, color=color, weight="bold")


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, ol_fs=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window. ol_fs: a smaller font for the two-letter
    line labels (LT, LG, RG, RT) on wide, full-field figures, where the default size overprints."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    if ol_fs:
        for t in fld.ax.texts:
            if t.get_text() in ("LT", "LG", "RG", "RT"):
                t.set_fontsize(ol_fs)
    return fld


def panel_title(ax, text, size=8.6):
    ax.set_title(text, loc="left", fontsize=size, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


# --- frame strips (print) and videos (web) for the simulated plays ---------------------------
MARK_R = 0.6   # smaller markers than the static diagrams so engaged players (about a yard apart) stay apart


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


RING_R = 0.9  # ring radius in the strips: big enough to see, small enough not to swallow a neighbour


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), hull=False, links=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play: markers, faint trails, rings, and optionally the pocket outline."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.4, play.los + window[1] - 0.4)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.4, yhi - 0.4)]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    if hull:
        draw_hull(fld, cur)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(7.5, ppy * (0.8 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.55)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), RING_R, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.7, zorder=7))
    for a, b in links:                      # dotted 'who has whom' lines between current positions
        pa = cur[cur["displayName"] == a].iloc[0]
        pb = cur[cur["displayName"] == b].iloc[0]
        xs, ys = fld.xy(np.array([pa["x"], pb["x"]]), np.array([pa["y"], pb["y"]]))
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=GREEN, lw=1.5, ls=(0, (1, 1.4)), zorder=9)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-9, 9), window=(-9, 6), ncols=4, rings=(), title=None,
          width_in=6.5, hull=False, final_links=()):
    """Numbered, captioned frame strip with a fixed box-sized window, so markers stay legible in print."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.55 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, hull, final_links if i == len(times) - 1 else ())
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"),
                     fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.02, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK, linespacing=1.15)
    if title:
        fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0 if notes else 0.5, w_pad=0.5)
    return fig


def video(play, times, notes=None, lateral=(-9, 9), window=(-9, 6), rings=(), width_in=5.4, hull=False):
    """Web version of the strip: every frame, with the strip's notes as running captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, hull)
        txt = "snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        if notes:
            cur = [n.replace("\n", " ") for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1]) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    frames = [f for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique()) if float(tmap[f]) >= -0.3]
    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=frames, interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def protection_animation(play, times, notes=None, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, notes=notes, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        video(play, times, notes=notes, **{k: v for k, v in kw.items() if k in ("lateral", "window", "rings", "hull")})


# --- the pocket as a shape: convex hull of the five linemen and the quarterback ---------------
def convex_hull(pts):
    """Monotone-chain convex hull of (x, y) points, counter-clockwise."""
    pts = sorted(set(map(tuple, np.round(np.asarray(pts, dtype=float), 4))))
    if len(pts) < 3:
        return np.array(pts)

    def cross(o, a, b):
        return (a[0] - o[0]) * (b[1] - o[1]) - (a[1] - o[1]) * (b[0] - o[0])
    lower, upper = [], []
    for q in pts:
        while len(lower) >= 2 and cross(lower[-2], lower[-1], q) <= 0:
            lower.pop()
        lower.append(q)
    for q in reversed(pts):
        while len(upper) >= 2 and cross(upper[-2], upper[-1], q) <= 0:
            upper.pop()
        upper.append(q)
    return np.array(lower[:-1] + upper[:-1])


def hull_area(h):
    x, y = h[:, 0], h[:, 1]
    return 0.5 * abs(np.dot(x, np.roll(y, -1)) - np.dot(y, np.roll(x, -1)))


def pocket_points(frame):
    """BDB (x, y) of the five linemen and the quarterback in one tracking frame."""
    sel = frame[frame["displayName"].isin(OL_KEYS + ["QB"])]
    return sel[["x", "y"]].to_numpy()


def draw_hull(fld, frame, color=GREEN):
    h = convex_hull(pocket_points(frame))
    xs, ys = fld.xy(h[:, 0], h[:, 1])
    fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(np.column_stack([xs, ys]), closed=True, fc=color, alpha=0.18, ec=color, lw=1.2,
                             zorder=2.5))
```

Third-and-7, late in the first half. The offense lines up with five receivers spread across the
field and nobody beside the quarterback. The defense walks two linebackers right up to the line,
one on each side of the center, and a slot cornerback creeps toward the edge. You count seven
defenders who might rush; the offense has five blockers. The center points and shouts a number.
The quarterback points somewhere else and shouts a different word. Then the ball is snapped, the
slot cornerback comes free off the edge, untouched, and the ball is already gone: a quick slant to the
slot receiver, caught in the space where the cornerback used to be. Nobody blocked the man who came
free, and that was the plan. This chapter is about why.

**You'll be able to:**

- Count rushers against blockers right after the snap, and say whether anyone was supposed to be
  free and who should have taken him.
- Name the protection from what the backs and tight ends do: slide or man, five, six, seven or eight
  blockers, check-release or chip.
- Explain why the offense names a "Mike" before the snap and what goes wrong when two blockers count
  from different men.
- Read the pocket: which linemen give ground and which must not, what a vertical or jump set is
  for, and why pressure up the middle hurts most.
- Explain how two linemen pass off a stunt, and why "stay with your man" loses to it.
- Read protection numbers (pressure rate, time to throw, sack rate) and say why a sack is not
  just the offensive line's fault.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[Passing Game Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)**: the quarterback's **drop**, the steps he
  takes back before he throws (three, five or seven from under center; one, three or five from the shotgun, where he
  already starts five yards deep), and the idea that routes are timed to it. Protection exists to make that
  timing possible.
- **[The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd)**: gaps A, B and C
  outward from the center, **technique numbers** (a **3-technique** lines up on the guard's outside shoulder,
  a **1-technique** shaded on the center), and *hat math*: counting blockers against defenders.
- **[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)**: the quarterback or center
  pointing at a linebacker and calling "54's the Mike!", and defenses moving after the offense has made its calls.
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and *left* and *right*
are always the offense's. The five offensive linemen are labelled LT, LG, C, RG and RT, Q is the
quarterback and R the running back; X, Z and H are wide receivers and Y (and U) tight ends. On defense, E is
an end, and the two defensive tackles are labelled by technique: **1** for the one shaded on the center,
**3** for the one on a guard's outside shoulder. M, W and S are the Mike, Will and Sam linebackers, NB the slot
(nickel) cornerback, C a cornerback, FS and SS the safeties. A line ending in a short bar is a block or a
**pass set** (the spot a blocker moves to at the snap to meet his rusher; more on sets later), an arrow a path,
a dotted green line "this blocker is responsible for that defender," and a shaded green oval a gap a lineman
owns. Rushers' paths are orange; a red dashed arrow is a rusher nobody blocks. A dotted orange line from a
defender to a receiver means man coverage, the dotted brown arrow is the ball in the air, and the solid orange
line across the field, where one is drawn, is the line to gain.

## Protection is counting

Start with the arithmetic, because every protection in this chapter is an answer to it.

On a pass, the offense always has five blockers: the five offensive linemen, who are not allowed to go out
for passes (they are *ineligible*) and so have nothing else to do. It may add more. A running back or a tight
end can stay in to block, making six, seven or even eight. Every extra blocker is one fewer receiver, and that
is the trade at the heart of the whole subject.

The defense, meanwhile, can rush anyone it likes. Most of the time it rushes four: in the 2024 and 2025
regular seasons about two dropbacks in three faced exactly four rushers, about one in five faced five, and
fewer than one in ten faced six or more.[^rushers] Four is the default for the reason
[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) gave: four rushers
leave seven defenders to cover at most five receivers. A [blitz](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
(sending a fifth, sixth or seventh rusher) flips that trade, giving up coverage to try to create a rusher the
offense cannot block.

So the offense's question on every pass is: **how many might come, how many can I block, and if the answer is
"not enough," who is left over?** Three ideas follow from it, and they organise the rest of the chapter.

**1. The protection does not have to win forever, only long enough.** A quarterback in today's NFL gets the ball
out in a little under three seconds on average (you will see the numbers at the end of the chapter). A
rusher who arrives at 3.5 seconds has not hurt anyone. Protection is a race against a clock, not a wrestling
match to the finish.

**2. Block inside-out.** Rushers from the middle of the line have the shortest path to the quarterback; rushers
from the edges have to run around the blockers. So when an offense must choose who to block and who to leave,
it blocks the inside man and leaves the widest one, because he has the longest way to go and the ball can be out
before he gets there.

**3. Someone left unblocked on purpose is the quarterback's.** If six come and the offense has five blockers,
one rusher is unblocked by design. That man is called a [**free rusher**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-rusher):
a rusher nobody is assigned to block. The protection does not fail when there is a free rusher; it hands him to
the quarterback, who must throw before he arrives. A free rusher who was *supposed* to be blocked is a different
thing: a bust, and you will learn to tell the two apart.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Pass protection exists because the defense chooses its numbers after the offense has chosen its own. The offense
commits its blockers in the huddle; the defense can show four rushers and bring six, or show six and bring three.
Every protection scheme is a set of rules that decides, after the snap, which blocker takes which rusher, so
that the most dangerous rushers are always blocked and any man left over is one the quarterback can beat with a
quick throw.
:::

## The pocket: a cup, not a wall

Before we can say who blocks whom, we need the shape of what they are protecting. The
[**pocket**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pocket) is the protected space the blockers form around the
quarterback, and the best way to picture it is a cup, not a wall.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pocket-geometry
#| fig-cap: "The pocket's shape, about a second after the snap (the quarterback is drawn at his launch point; backs and receivers are not shown). The interior linemen take short sets, only a yard or so back, and hold firm; the tackles kick back several yards so the ends must run an arc around them. That arc is far longer than the 3-technique's straight path up the middle, which is why the edge can be pushed past the quarterback while the middle must not give an inch, and why the quarterback steps up into the cup rather than drifting back."
p = Play(line() + gun(None, qb_d=-7.5), four_down(lbs=False), los=35, to_go=None,
         title="The pocket is a cup, not a wall")
SETS = {"LT": (-3.6, -4.4), "LG": (-2.0, -1.8), "C": (-1.6, 0.0), "RG": (-2.0, 1.8), "RT": (-3.6, 4.4)}
for k, sp in SETS.items():
    to(p, k, sp)
to(p, "LE", (-6.6, -3.4), "rush", via=[(-1.2, -6.1), (-4.6, -5.9)])
to(p, "RE", (-6.6, 3.4), "rush", via=[(-1.2, 6.1), (-4.6, 5.9)])
to(p, "NT", (-1.0, -1.1), "rush"); to(p, "DT", (-1.1, 2.1), "rush")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-12, 12), window=(-12, 4.2))
cup = [(-3.6, -4.4), (-2.0, -1.8), (-1.6, 0.0), (-2.0, 1.8), (-3.6, 4.4), (-8.6, 3.0), (-9.6, 0.0), (-8.6, -3.0)]
xy = np.array([_P(fld, p, d, w) for d, w in cup], dtype=float)
fld.ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=GREEN, alpha=0.13, ec=GREEN, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1.5))
(x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, -6.6, 0.0), _P(fld, p, -5.0, 0.0)
fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=GREEN, lw=1.8,
                                 zorder=9))
say(fld, p, -5.6, 1.9, "step up", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (-10.3, -4.0), (-7.5, 0.0), "launch point\n(about 7-8 yd deep)")
# path lengths: the end's arc around the tackle vs the 3-technique's straight line to the launch point
arc = [(1.0, -5.0), (-1.2, -6.1), (-4.6, -5.9), (-6.6, -3.4), (-7.5, 0.0)]
edge = sum(np.hypot(b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]) for a, b in zip(arc[:-1], arc[1:]))
inside = np.hypot(1.0 + 7.5, 2.35)
point_to(fld, p, (2.75, -7.6), (1.0, -5.0), f"edge rusher: about {edge:.0f} yd\naround the tackle", shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (2.75, 4.6), (1.0, 2.35), f"3-technique: about {inside:.0f} yd\nstraight up the middle", shrink=9)
for side in (-1, 1):
    say(fld, p, -5.0, side * 9.6, "tackles give\nground and push\nthe edge past", fontsize=7, color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, -3.6, 0.0, "interior: hold firm", fontsize=7, color=GREEN)
plt.show()
```

Three facts about the cup explain most of pass protection.

**The quarterback throws from a spot, and the linemen know where it is.** The
[**launch point**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-launch-point) is where the quarterback sets his feet to throw
at the end of his drop. From the shotgun he starts five yards deep and takes a short drop, so on a typical
dropback he throws from about seven or eight yards behind the line; from under center a five-step drop ends at a
similar depth and a seven-step drop deeper.[^depth] Linemen set their depth to that spot. The aim is not to stop
every rusher at the line; it is to keep every rusher off *that spot* until the ball is gone. When a play-action
pass or a rollout moves the launch point, the whole line's geometry changes with it, which is why those plays have
their own protections ([Play-Action, Bootlegs and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)).

**The interior must not give ground.** Look at the distances in @fig-pocket-geometry. A defensive tackle rushing
straight up the middle is about nine yards from the launch point. An end rushing around the tackle has to run
an arc of about thirteen. So the guards and center set only a step or two back and then hold, because every yard
they give is a yard straight into the quarterback's face. Pressure up the middle is the most destructive kind:
the quarterback cannot step up into it, cannot see over it, and cannot escape it by moving forward.

**The tackles give ground on purpose.** The tackles retreat several yards, backward and outward, keeping
themselves between the end and the quarterback. If the end keeps running his arc, the tackle runs with him and
pushes him *past* the launch point, deeper than the quarterback, where he is no threat. That is why a
quarterback with a good pocket **steps up**: he moves forward into the cup as the edge rushers are pushed behind
him. Stepping up is a skill the [quarterback chapter](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) builds on; for now, notice that
it only works if the interior held. A quarterback who drifts *backward* instead runs into the ends the tackles were
pushing past him.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The offensive line should form a wall." A flat wall at the line of scrimmage would be beaten at both ends in a
second, because the edge rushers would simply run around it. The pocket is deliberately bent: firm in the
middle, deep at the edges, with the quarterback inside the bend. When you see a tackle five yards behind the
line with a defensive end running past him, that is usually the protection working, not failing.
:::

## Two ways to block five: slide and man

Now the assignments. There are two basic ways to decide which blocker takes which rusher, and every protection in
the NFL is one of them or a mix of the two. They are the pass-protection cousins of the two run-blocking
philosophies in [03-01](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd): blocking an *area* and blocking a *man*.

```{python}
#| label: fig-slide-vs-man
#| fig-cap: "The same six blockers against the same front, two ways (receivers and defensive backs not shown). Left, slide right: each lineman takes the gap to his right (shaded), whoever comes through it, so the 1-technique belongs to the LG, the 3-technique to the RG and the right end to the RT; the Mike or Will, if they blitz, run into the C's or LT's gap. The slide leaves the left end behind, so the back takes him. Right, man protection, also called BOB (big-on-big): the linemen take the four defensive linemen and the Mike, and the back takes the Will."
LAT, WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-6.8, 6.4)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.7))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("slide", "man")):
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if kind == "slide":
        for k, wg in zip(OL_KEYS, (-2.4, -0.8, 0.8, 2.4, 4.0)):
            to(p, k, (-0.25, wg - 0.15))
        to(p, "RB", (-3.6, -3.9))
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    if kind == "slide":
        for wg in (-2.4, -0.8, 0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
            gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "LE")
        panel_title(ax, "Slide right: each lineman owns a gap")
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -0.2, "the gap to my right,\nwhoever comes", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -5.2, -4.6, "back: the end\nleft behind", color=GREEN)
    else:
        for k, m in zip(OL_KEYS + ["RB"], ("LE", "NT", "MIKE", "DT", "RE", "WILL")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Man (BOB): each blocker owns a man")
        say(fld, p, -3.6, 4.2, "linemen: the four\nlinemen + the Mike", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -5.4, -4.6, "back: the Will", color=GREEN)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

**Slide protection.** In [**slide protection**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection) every lineman
takes his first step the same way and owns the gap on that side, *whoever* comes through it. In the left panel
of @fig-slide-vs-man the line slides right: the left tackle owns the gap between himself and the left guard, the
left guard the gap between himself and the center, and so on across to the right tackle, who owns the space
outside himself. Notice that nobody on the line has to know in advance which defender will rush where. If the
1-technique rushes, he is in the left guard's gap; if instead the Will linebacker blitzes and the 1-technique drops
into coverage (defenses do this; see [Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)),
the left tackle's gap gets the Will and the left guard's gap gets nobody, and the left guard helps a neighbor.

The price of sliding one way is the man on the other end. Five linemen sliding right cover five gaps, from the
left B gap to outside the right tackle, and that leaves the left end, outside everyone, uncovered. Someone else has
to take him: the running back in the picture, or a tight end. That is the slide's weak spot. The man it leaves
behind is usually a defensive end, often the defense's best pass rusher, and now a 215-pound back has him.

So the direction of the slide is a decision, and it follows one rule of thumb: **the slide goes where the
trouble is inside, and never leaves a star alone with a back.** Offenses slide toward the most dangerous inside
rusher, or toward the side with more possible rushers (an *overload*). If the defense's best player is an edge
rusher, they slide *away* from him and block him with the tackle man to man (the half-slide coming up next does
exactly this), then add a chip (later in this chapter) on top. Help is always *in addition to* the tackle, never
instead of him.

**Man protection.** In [**man protection**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-protection), each blocker is
given a specific defender before the snap. The usual rule is the one in the right panel: the five linemen take
the four defensive linemen plus one linebacker, and the back takes the other linebacker. Line coaches call it
"big on big" ([**BOB**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bob), or
[**big-on-big**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-big-on-big)), because the big men block the big men, and the back
is left with a linebacker, a fairer fight than a defensive end.

Man protection matches strength to strength, and it handles a four-man rush cleanly. Its weakness is movement.
If two defenders cross paths after the snap (a [**stunt**](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd), coming up later in
this chapter), each man-blocker must chase his man through traffic. If a linebacker the line was counting on drops
out and a different one rushes, the assignments are wrong for the rusher who actually came. Slide protection
shrugs off both, because a gap does not move. That is the trade, and it is the same one zone and gap blocking
make in the run game: man blocking wins the one-on-one matchups it planned for; area blocking survives the ones
it did not.

## Half-slide: the NFL's everyday six-man protection

Most real protections split the difference. In a [**half-slide**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-half-slide)
the center and the two linemen on one side slide that way and block gaps, the two linemen on the other side block
man-to-man, and the running back takes the first extra rusher on the man side. This is the "60" protection from
the play call you decoded in [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd), and some
version of it is the most common six-man protection in football. (Many playbooks number their protections in
families, "50s," "60s," "90s," with the number saying which way the slide goes and who blocks; others use words.
What each number means differs from team to team.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-half-slide
#| fig-cap: "Half-slide right against a four-man rush (receivers and defensive backs not shown). The C, RG and RT slide right and own the shaded gaps; the LG and LT block the man in front of them; the back's job is the Will. Here both linebackers drop into coverage, so nobody comes into the center's gap and nobody comes for the back: the center helps the left guard on the 1-technique, and the back, having checked the Will, slips out into a route. Six blockers have become five against four, with a spare, plus a sixth receiver."
p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), four_down(), los=35, to_go=None,
         title="Half-slide right against a four-man rush")
to(p, "C", (-1.8, -0.75), via=[(-1.8, 0.45)])
for k, wg in zip(["RG", "RT"], (2.4, 4.0)):
    to(p, k, (-0.25, wg - 0.15))
to(p, "LT", (-1.6, -4.3)); to(p, "LG", (-1.2, -1.2))
to(p, "LE", (-1.4, -5.6), "rush", via=[(0.0, -5.6)])
to(p, "RE", (-1.4, 5.6), "rush", via=[(0.0, 5.6)])
to(p, "NT", (0.1, -0.85), "rush"); to(p, "DT", (0.1, 2.3), "rush")
p.drop("MIKE", (9.0, 2.0)); p.drop("WILL", (8.5, -4.5))
to(p, "RB", (-1.0, -6.6), "route", via=[(-3.8, -2.6)])
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-9.5, 9.5), window=(-7.2, 10.4))
for wg in (0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
    gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
for k, m in (("LT", "LE"), ("LG", "NT")):
    assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.7, 3.7), (-1.8, 0.3), "C: no one came into\nhis gap, so he helps", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 2.9, 4.4, "slide side", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.9, -4.4, "man side", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (-5.8, -6.4), (-3.8, -2.6), "back: checks the Will,\nthen releases", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 8.8, -6.9, "Will drops", fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 9.2, 4.4, "Mike drops", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

Walk through @fig-half-slide. On the right, the slide side, the center, right guard and right tackle each own a
gap, so any combination of the 3-technique, the right end and the Mike linebacker is accounted for. On the left,
the man side, the guard has the 1-technique and the tackle has the left end. The back watches the Will. Count it:
six blockers for six possible rushers (four linemen, two linebackers), with every gap and every man covered once.

The half-slide is popular because it gives each part of the line the job it is best at. The slide side handles
the movement defenses love to run inside (stunts, linebackers looping through gaps). The man side keeps the
offense's tackle on the defensive end, big on big, rather than handing that end to the back. And the back gets
the defender with the longest path, an off-the-ball linebacker, whom he can meet in the hole.

Against the four-man rush in the picture, both linebackers dropped. The protection does not care: the center
had nobody in his gap, so he "looks for work" and helps a neighbor (here the left guard on the 1-technique), and
the back, whose man did not come, runs a route. Six blockers turned into five plus a receiver. That last move
is called check-release, and it is one of the most important things a back does; it gets its own section below.

Why would anyone still call a full slide, then? Because it puts all five linemen on gaps, and gaps are the
answer to movement. Against a front that loves stunts, or that stacks linebackers to come through the A and B
gaps, a full slide toward the pressure means no lineman has to chase anybody; the offense accepts the cost (a back
or tight end on the backside end) because the inside threat is the bigger one.

**How to tell which one you are watching.** On the broadcast, look at the linemen's first step after the snap.
All five step the same way: a slide. The center and the two linemen on one side step together while the other
two set straight back at the man in front of them: a half-slide, with the slide toward the center's step. Each
lineman sets to a different defender, some stepping left and some right: man.

## Mike identification: counting from the same man

Every protection above depends on everyone agreeing which linebacker is which. The half-slide said "the back
takes the Will," and the man protection "the linemen take the four linemen and the Mike." But the defense does
not wear name tags, and linebackers move. So before the snap one player makes the call you heard in
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd): "54's the Mike!" That call is
[**Mike identification**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-identification), often written
[**MIKE ID**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-id). In most offenses the quarterback has the final word,
because he sees the whole defense; in others the center, who is closest to the front and runs the line's
communication, makes it.[^count]

### How the count works

The "Mike" in the call is a **reference point**, not necessarily the defense's real middle linebacker. Every
assignment is written relative to him, so naming him turns six separate judgments ("which one is mine?") into
one decision that everyone follows. Systems differ in the details, but one common way to build a six-man
protection around the call, the one in @fig-the-count, works like this.

1. **The center works toward the Mike.** He and the two linemen on that side slide that way and own the gaps
   there, so the Mike (call him 0) and anyone on his side belong to the slide.
2. **The other two linemen count outward from the Mike on their side.** The guard takes the first defender on the
   line (1), the tackle the second (2). This is the man side.
3. **The back takes the next threat beyond the line's count** (3), usually the linebacker on the man side. If he
   rushes, the back blocks him; if he drops, the back releases. In many playbooks the back has two men to check
   in order, inside first (a *dual read*), and takes whichever comes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-the-count
#| fig-cap: "The count, number by number (receivers and defensive backs not shown; the linebackers are labelled by jersey number). Left: \"54's the Mike.\" The center works toward 54, so the C, RG and RT slide right and own the shaded gaps; 54 is 0 and belongs to the slide. On the man side the guard takes the first defender on the line (1), the tackle the second (2), and the back the linebacker beyond them (3). Right: the same defense, but the quarterback names 52 instead. Now the slide goes left, the RG and RT take the 3-technique and the end man to man, and the back's man is 54, on the other side of the quarterback: he has to block across the quarterback's face, which takes him longer."
LAT, WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-7.4, 6.8)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
for ax, mike in zip(axes, ("54", "52")):
    dfn = [q.moved(label="54") if q.key == "MIKE" else q.moved(label="52") if q.key == "WILL" else q
           for q in four_down(will=(4.5, -2.6))]
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    if mike == "52":
        to(p, "RB", (-3.4, 1.7), via=[(-4.0, -0.5)])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    if mike == "54":
        for wg in (0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
            gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
        tag(fld, p, "MIKE", "0"); tag(fld, p, "NT", "1"); tag(fld, p, "LE", "2"); tag(fld, p, "WILL", "3")
        for k, m in (("LG", "NT"), ("LT", "LE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "WILL", lw=1.6, via=[(-2.4, -2.4)])
        panel_title(ax, "1  \"54's the Mike!\"")
        say(fld, p, -2.9, 4.6, "slide side:\n0 and his side,\nby gaps", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -3.2, -4.8, "man side:\nG takes 1, T takes 2", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -6.2, -4.2, "back: 3", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
    else:
        for wg in (-0.8, -2.4, -4.0):
            gap_oval(fld, p, wg)
        tag(fld, p, "WILL", "0"); tag(fld, p, "DT", "1"); tag(fld, p, "RE", "2"); tag(fld, p, "MIKE", "3")
        for k, m in (("RG", "DT"), ("RT", "RE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        panel_title(ax, "2  The quarterback names 52")
        say(fld, p, -2.9, -4.6, "slide side:\n0 and his side,\nby gaps", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -6.2, 4.0, "back: 3, across\nthe QB's face", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

Numbered like that, the call does all the work, and the right panel shows its power: change the name and the
slide flips, the guard and tackle on the man side have new men, and the back's man moves to the other side. So the
call is also a tool. A quarterback who sees a threat gathering on one side can name a defender over there, which
pulls the slide, and its linemen, toward the threat, so that a lineman rather than the back is responsible for
the most dangerous rusher. The cost of all this is time and noise: every call has to be heard by five or six
men, on the road, with the play clock running.

The right panel also answers a question about the back. In most half-slides he lines up on the man side, the
side he will check, so he has a short trip. When the call puts his man on the other side, he has to block
**across the quarterback's face**, in front of him to the other side, which takes longer. So the back's
alignment is a clue to the protection, not a guarantee. Watch where he steps at the snap.

That is what happened in the opening scene. The center pointed and called a number: his Mike, one of the two
linebackers standing in the A gaps. The quarterback, who has the final word, pointed elsewhere and called a word
of his own, a code that set which way the line would work and so which side the unblocked rusher would come from.
That also told the slot receiver on that side that he was the answer. (The words are code and change from team to
team; some staffs use one word for each direction, others fold the direction into a protection number.)

```{python}
#| label: fig-mike-count
#| fig-cap: "Why one player names the Mike (receivers and defensive backs not shown; the linebackers are labelled by jersey number). Left: the call is \"54's the Mike,\" so the linemen take the four defensive linemen plus 54, and the back takes 52; every possible rusher has exactly one blocker. Right: the same defense, but the center counted from 52 instead. He turns to 52, the back also takes 52, and when 54 blitzes the right A gap nobody is responsible for him. The defense rushed no more men than the offense had blockers; the free rusher came from two blockers counting from different men."
LAT, WIN = (-7.2, 7.2), (-7.4, 6.6)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
for ax, bust in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    dfn = [q.moved(label="54") if q.key == "MIKE" else q.moved(label="52") if q.key == "WILL" else q
           for q in four_down(will=(4.5, -2.9))]
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=LAT, window=WIN)
    if not bust:
        for k, m in zip(OL_KEYS, ("LE", "NT", "MIKE", "DT", "RE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "WILL", lw=1.6, via=[(-2.4, -2.5)])
        panel_title(ax, "1  One call: \"54's the Mike!\"")
        say(fld, p, -3.3, 4.3, "line: the four linemen\n+ 54 (the Mike)", color=GREEN)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, -3.9, "back: 52", color=GREEN)
    else:
        for k, m in (("LT", "LE"), ("LG", "NT"), ("RG", "DT"), ("RT", "RE")):
            assign(fld, p, k, m, lw=1.6)
        assign(fld, p, "RB", "WILL", lw=1.6, via=[(-2.4, -2.5)])
        assign(fld, p, "C", "WILL", lw=1.6, color=RED, via=[(0.6, -1.9)])
        free_path(fld, p, [(4.5, 1.2), (0.2, 0.75), (-4.0, 0.3)], label="54: free", label_at=(-2.6, 2.6))
        panel_title(ax, "2  The center thought 52 was the Mike")
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -5.0, "two blockers\non 52", color=RED)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

@fig-mike-count shows what happens when the count is not shared: the defense rushed only five men against six
blockers and still got a man free, because two blockers counted from different starting points. This is the
classic **bust**, and when you see a linebacker run untouched through the middle against a normal-looking rush,
it is the first thing to suspect. (Re-declaring the Mike when a defender walks up late, which you met in
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd), is the offense's attempt to keep the count
shared after the defense has moved.)

Some quarterbacks make this part of their game. Tom Brady was known for it: his Mike calls are audible on
broadcasts, and teammates describe him overruling the line's identification at the line of scrimmage ("no,
*he's* the Mike") to move the protection toward a matchup he did not like, then getting the ball out to the hot
receiver before a free rusher arrived.[^brady] The skill is invisible on most broadcasts, and it is part of why
analysts treat sack rate as partly a quarterback statistic, not only a line statistic.

Defenses know this, which is why they move after the call. Linebackers walk up into the A gaps at the last
second, safeties rotate down, a lineman stands up and drops back. Each move is an attempt to make the offense's
count wrong after it is too late to fix. The two-linebacker version, both standing in the A gaps on either
side of the center, is the "double A-gap mug" of [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd),
and it exists almost entirely to attack the Mike call: with both linebackers threatening the middle, which one is
the Mike? Here, in miniature, is why the pre-snap phase looks like the busiest few seconds in sport.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden you can tap a button to "slide protection left" or tell the back to block, and the computer linemen
then know exactly who to block. Real linemen have to agree on it, out loud, in a few seconds, in a stadium
built to drown them out, while the defense rearranges itself to make their agreement wrong. Most of what makes
an NFL offensive line "good" in the eyes of coaches is invisible on a broadcast: not strength, but five players
reaching the same answer at the same time, snap after snap.
:::

## The back and the tight end: check-release and chip

The running back in a six-man protection is the part of the protection you can see most easily, and his job
is the subtlest. He has a defender to watch, not a defender to block, and he finds out after the snap which job
he has. That rule is called [**check-release**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-release): check your man;
if he rushes, block him; if he does not, release into your route. The animation shows the "he rushes" half.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rb-pickup
#| fig-cap: "Check-release, when the check comes (simulated). Half-slide right as in the earlier figure, but this time the Will (ringed in purple) blitzes through the left B gap while the Mike drops. The back (ringed in green) keeps his eyes on the Will from the snap, steps up, and meets him in the hole between the left guard and left tackle, so five rushers face six blockers and the pocket holds. Had the Will dropped, the back would have released into his route."
def pickup_play():
    p = Play(line() + gun(-1.5), four_down(), los=35, to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.9, -7.4, 0.0)])
    # the four linemen rush; each is met by the blocker the half-slide gives him
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.5, -0.6, -5.9), (1.0, -2.3, -6.0), (2.0, -3.5, -5.8)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.7, -4.2), (1.0, -2.8, -4.8), (2.0, -3.9, -4.6)], "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.5, 0.0, -0.9), (1.0, -0.5, -0.9), (2.0, -0.9, -0.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.5, -1.3, -1.5), (1.0, -1.7, -1.2), (2.0, -2.1, -1.1)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.5, -1.4, 0.3), (1.0, -1.8, 0.4), (2.0, -2.2, 0.4)], "block")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.5, 0.0, 2.3), (1.0, -0.6, 2.2), (2.0, -0.9, 2.1)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.5, -1.3, 1.8), (1.0, -1.8, 1.9), (2.0, -2.1, 1.9)], "block")
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.5, -0.6, 5.7), (1.0, -2.3, 5.6), (2.0, -3.5, 5.3)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.5, -1.7, 4.0), (1.0, -2.8, 4.4), (2.0, -3.9, 4.2)], "block")
    # the Will blitzes the left B gap; the Mike drops
    timed(p, "WILL", [(0.5, 1.9, -2.7), (1.0, -0.6, -3.0), (2.0, -1.0, -3.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "MIKE", [(1.0, 6.5, 1.5), (2.0, 8.0, 1.8)], "path")
    # the back: eyes on the Will, steps up and meets him in the hole, a yard or two behind the line
    timed(p, "RB", [(0.5, -4.2, -2.3), (1.0, -2.3, -3.0), (2.0, -2.6, -3.0)], "block")
    return p


protection_animation(pickup_play(), [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0],
    notes=["snap: six blockers;\nthe back watches W", "W blitzes the B gap;\nthe back steps up",
           "the back meets him\nin the hole", "five rushers, six blockers:\nthe pocket holds"],
    lateral=(-7.5, 6.5), window=(-8.6, 6.4), ncols=2, rings=(("RB", style.THIRD), ("WILL", PURPLE)))
```

Three details in @fig-rb-pickup are worth noticing, because they are what coaches grade backs on.

**His eyes go to the linebacker, not the quarterback.** At the snap the back is looking at the Will. He has a
fraction of a second to decide, and a back who looks at the quarterback first, or at the ball, will be late.

**He steps up to meet the blitzer.** The back attacks forward into the gap rather than waiting for the linebacker
to arrive at the quarterback's feet. Meeting him in the hole, a yard or two behind the line and well in front of
the quarterback, keeps the collision away from the launch point and gives the linebacker less room to run around
him.

**He takes on a bigger, faster-moving man.** A linebacker on a blitz may outweigh the back by 20 pounds and is
running at full speed; the back is standing nearly still. That is why "can he pass protect?" is one of the first
questions asked about a rookie running back, and why a back who can't is often taken off the field on third
down, however well he runs.

The other half of the rule, the release, is what makes the six-man protection efficient. A back who stays in
to block nobody has wasted a receiver. With check-release, the offense gets a blocker when it needs one and a
receiver when it doesn't, and it finds out which only after the defense has committed. Tight ends play by the
same rule when they are part of the protection.

Two refinements, both about order. When a back has more than one man to check (the dual read above), he looks
inside first, because the inside blitzer has the shorter path. And when the play also asks him to chip, the order
is fixed: **check, then chip, then release.** The blitz comes first, because a blitzer is a free man and an end
already has a tackle on him.

### The chip: help on the way out

Between "block" and "release" there is a third option. A [**chip**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-chip) is a
quick shove by a tight end or back on a pass rusher, usually an edge rusher, delivered on the way out into his
route. It is not a block. It is a hit, a second at most, aimed at knocking the rusher off his path or breaking
his rhythm, so that the tackle can catch up with him.

```{python}
#| label: fig-chip
#| fig-cap: "Chip, then release (the outside receivers are not shown). Y lines up as a wing, a step outside and behind the left tackle, with the left end wider still (a wide alignment coaches call a 9-technique); the back stands to the quarterback's right. At the snap each hits the nearest end from the inside as he starts his rush (the stars), knocking him wider and slowing him for the tackle, and then runs his route: Y up the seam, the back to the flat. The back has checked first that no linebacker is blitzing (check, chip, release). The offense gets help against two pass rushers and still gets two receivers out, just a beat later."
off = line() + gun(1.5) + [O("Y", "TE", -1.2, -4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                           O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 15.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -6.3, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.3, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, 1.0, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.8, -2.6, "W")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None, title="Chip, then release")
to(p, "LE", (-3.4, -5.6), "rush", via=[(-0.5, -6.8)])
to(p, "RE", (-3.6, 5.2), "rush", via=[(-1.0, 6.0)])
to(p, "LT", (-2.9, -4.6)); to(p, "RT", (-3.0, 4.3))
to(p, "NT", (0.1, -0.85), "rush"); to(p, "DT", (0.1, 2.3), "rush")
to(p, "LG", (-1.3, -1.3)); to(p, "C", (-1.4, 0.0)); to(p, "RG", (-1.3, 1.9))
to(p, "Y", (8.0, -6.6), "route", via=[(-0.4, -5.9), (2.4, -5.6)])
to(p, "RB", (0.0, 9.2), "route", via=[(-2.6, 5.4), (-1.8, 7.0)])
p.drop("MIKE", (9.5, 1.5)); p.drop("WILL", (9.0, -3.5))
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-11.5, 11.5), window=(-7.4, 11.4))
for (d, w) in ((-0.4, -5.9), (-2.6, 5.4)):
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="*", ms=13, color=style.THIRD, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=11)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.6, -7.6), (-0.4, -5.9), "Y chips the end\nfrom the inside\n(a shove, not a block)", color=GREEN)
point_to(fld, p, (-5.4, 7.8), (-2.6, 5.4), "the back chips\nthe other end", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 5.8, -8.6, "...then up\nthe seam", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, 2.4, 8.4, "...then\nthe flat", color=GREEN)
plt.show()
```

The chip exists because of the slide's weak spot and the defense's best player. When a defense has one edge
rusher the tackle cannot handle alone, the offense has three choices: leave the tackle on an island and hope,
keep a tight end in to block the rusher full-time (and lose a receiver), or chip him (and lose a beat on the
route). The chip is the cheap version of help. Its cost is timing: a receiver who chips is late into his route, so
chips go with routes that do not need to be on time, like a back's
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown) to the flat (the short, safe throw a quarterback makes when
nothing downfield is open) or a tight end's route underneath. And the chip comes from the inside, knocking the end
wider and deeper, the direction the tackle is already pushing him; a chip that drives him inside would push him
straight at the quarterback.

## More blockers, fewer receivers: max protect

Add a tight end to a six-man protection and you have a **seven-man protection**: the five linemen, the back and
a tight end. It usually stays flexible. The tight end and back check, chip and release, so three receivers are out
on time and one or two more arrive late, and its most common job is the one you just saw: putting help on
a dangerous edge rusher.

At the far end of the counting spectrum is [**max protect**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-max-protect). The
difference is not only the number but the commitment: seven or eight blockers who stay in to block *whatever the
defense does*, no check-releases, with only two or three receivers in the pattern. It is the offense's way of
buying the most time it can, and it nearly always travels with a deep throw.

```{python}
#| label: fig-max-protect
#| fig-cap: "Max protect from two tight ends (12 personnel), under center with a seven-step drop (Q is shown at the snap; the dotted line behind him is his drop, about nine yards deep). Eight men block (the five linemen, both tight ends U and Y, and the back R) against five rushers, so three blockers are spare and help wherever a rusher is winning. Only X and Z run routes, a deep post and a deep crossing route at about 14 yards, into six defenders in coverage. The offense has bought time, and spent receivers to do it: the play works only if one of those two gets open deep."
off = [q.moved(label=q.key) if q.key in OL_KEYS else q for q in offense("ace")]
off = [q.moved(w=-10.0) if q.key == "X" else q.moved(w=10.0) if q.key == "Z" else q for q in off]
dfn = [q.moved(label={"WDT": "1", "SDT": "3"}.get(q.key, q.label))
       for q in defense("4-3_over", "single_high", off)]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10, title="Max protect: eight block, two go deep")
p.dropback(8.5)
to(p, "RB", (-4.6, -1.6), "block")
to(p, "WDE", (-2.0, -5.0), "rush", via=[(0.0, -4.6)])
to(p, "WDT", (-0.2, -1.0), "rush"); to(p, "SDT", (-0.2, 2.3), "rush"); to(p, "SDE", (-0.3, 4.0), "rush")
to(p, "WILL", (0.2, -2.6), "rush")
# the linemen and tight ends set only a step (not drawn, so their labels stay readable)
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (9, 0), (15.0, -4.0)]); p.route("Z", [(0, 0), (14.0, 0), (14.0, -9.0)])
p.drop("MIKE", (10.0, 1.0)); p.drop("SAM", (9.5, 7.5)); p.drop("SS", (11.0, 4.0))
p.drop("LCB", (12.5, -10.5)); p.drop("RCB", (12.5, 10.5)); p.drop("FS", (15.5, 0.0))
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-12.6, 12.6), window=(-11.8, 17.6), ol_fs=6.2)
say(fld, p, -5.4, -8.6, "8 blockers\nvs 5 rushers", color=GREEN, fontsize=8, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -4.6, 8.4, "2 receivers\nvs 6 in coverage", color=RED, fontsize=8, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (-8.2, 6.0), (-1.2, 4.0), "spare blockers\nlook for work", color=GREEN)
point_to(fld, p, (-9.0, -5.0), (-4.6, -1.6), "the back stays in", color=GREEN)
point_to(fld, p, (-10.3, 4.2), (-10.4, 0.3), "Q's launch point", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

Max protect exists because deep routes take time. A 20-yard post needs the quarterback to hold the ball for three
seconds or more, and against a good rush that time has to be bought with bodies. It pairs naturally with
[**play-action**](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd) (a fake handoff before the pass), because the
heavy formation and the extra blockers look exactly like a run, which freezes the linebackers and safeties for the
half-second the deep routes need.

The trade is stark, and @fig-max-protect puts numbers on it. With eight blocking and five rushing, the
quarterback has all the time he wants. But two receivers against six defenders in coverage means double coverage
somewhere, and nowhere to go if both are covered except the sideline, a scramble or a sack. Max protect is a bet
that one of two receivers will beat his man deep. It is a good bet against a defense that has to respect the run
and a bad one against a defense that just drops eight.

## Fewer blockers, more receivers: scat and empty

At the other end are protections that block with five, or as close to five as possible, so that more players can
run routes.

In [**empty protection**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-empty-protection-five-man), the offense lines up with nobody
in the backfield except the quarterback (the "empty" formations of
[Spread and Modern Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)), so the
five linemen are the whole protection. Many teams block it man-to-man, the four defensive linemen plus the Mike;
others run it as a five-man slide or half-slide. Either way, any sixth rusher is the quarterback's problem.

In [**scat protection**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-scat-protection), the back lines up in the backfield, so
the defense has to respect him as a blocker, but he releases into his route at the snap instead of checking a
blitzer first. The line blocks, and as in empty, an extra rusher is the quarterback's.[^scat] Teams use the word in
different ways (in some playbooks "scat" is one numbered protection, in others a tag that can be added to several),
so treat it as "six in the picture, five in the protection."

Both exist for the same reason: five receivers stretch a defense further than four, and the quickest throws
come out before an extra rusher could arrive anyway. The quick game of [04-03](04-03-quick-game.qmd) is built on
this: a ball out in a second and a half makes a sixth rusher irrelevant. And both carry the same obligation. If the
defense sends one more than the protection can block, somebody has to get the ball out, now.

## When rushers outnumber blockers: hot routes and sight adjusts

That obligation is the last piece of the protection puzzle. When six rush and five block, the protection has
done its job if the man left over is the *right* man, the one with the longest path, and the rest of the
answer belongs to the quarterback and his receivers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-hot-throw
#| fig-cap: "Six rush, five block: the throw goes hot. The offense is in an empty 3x2 formation, so its five linemen are the whole protection; they take the four defensive linemen and the Mike. The defense brings a sixth rusher, the nickel back (NB) from over H, and plays man coverage behind it with one deep safety. Blocking inside-out leaves the nickel, the widest rusher with the longest path, unblocked by design (red). The answer is the hot throw: H breaks inside into the space the blitzer just left, and the ball is out before the nickel gets home."
def empty_3x2():
    """Empty backfield, 3x2: X and H on the left, Y, the back (R) and Z on the right."""
    return line() + gun(None) + [O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, -8.0),
                                 O("RB", "RB", -1.4, 6.5, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -1.4, 10.0), O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 14.0)]


def cover1_pressure():
    """Six rushers (four linemen, the Mike, the nickel back over H) and man coverage behind them."""
    return four_down(will=(4.5, 6.3)) + [
        D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -7.6, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 14.0, "C"),
        D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]


p = Play(empty_3x2(), cover1_pressure(), los=35, to_go=8, title="Six rush, five block: the throw goes hot")
p.dropback(1.0)
to(p, "LT", (-1.7, -4.3)); to(p, "RT", (-1.7, 4.3))     # interior sets are a step: not drawn
to(p, "LE", (-1.0, -5.6), "rush", via=[(0.0, -5.6)]); to(p, "RE", (-1.0, 5.6), "rush", via=[(0.0, 5.6)])
to(p, "NT", (0.2, -0.9), "rush"); to(p, "DT", (0.2, 2.25), "rush"); to(p, "MIKE", (0.6, 0.7), "rush")
p.route("H", [(0, 0), (1.5, 0), (5.0, -4.5)]); p.pass_to("H", t=0.95)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, [(0, 0), (6, 0), (5.4, -0.6)])
p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (12, -0.5)]); p.route("RB", [(0, 0), (5, 0), (5, 4)])
for d_, r_ in (("LCB", "X"), ("RCB", "Z"), ("SS", "Y"), ("WILL", "RB")):
    p.man(d_, r_)
p.drop("FS", (15.0, 0.0))
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-8.8, 16.6), ol_fs=6.2)
blitz = [(4.5, -7.6), (1.0, -6.6), (-3.6, -4.0), (-5.2, -1.2)]
free_path(fld, p, blitz)
run = sum(np.hypot(b[0] - a[0], b[1] - a[1]) for a, b in zip(blitz[:-1], blitz[1:]))
say(fld, p, 2.4, -11.6, "free rusher:\nthe nickel back", color=RED, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (8.6, -7.0), (3.4, -5.1), "hot: H breaks into the\nspace the blitzer left", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, -6.0, 8.5, "5 blockers: the four\nlinemen + the Mike", color=GREEN)
say(fld, p, -6.6, -10.2, f"ball out in about 1 s;\nthe blitzer has about\n{run:.0f} yd to run, close to 2 s", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

A [**hot route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route) is the throw built into a play for exactly this
moment: when a rusher comes that the protection cannot block, the quarterback throws at once to a receiver
running into the area that rusher just left. The logic is simple and a little beautiful. A defender who rushes is a
defender who is not covering, so the space he came from is, for a second or so, empty. In @fig-hot-throw the
nickel back was the man over H; when he blitzes, H's quick inside break runs straight into the hole. The
quarterback does not have to read the coverage; he has to recognise the blitz and be on time.

That is why "who's hot?" is part of the design of most dropback passes, not something made up on the field. The
play call and the protection together decide it: once the offense knows which rusher it will leave unblocked if
everyone comes, it knows which receiver's route has to be ready early. Usually the hot receiver is the man whose
defender is most likely to blitz (a slot receiver against a slot-cornerback blitz, a tight end against a
linebacker blitz). The quarterback's pre-snap job is to see whether the hot is live on this snap; a play whose
protection can block everyone who might come needs no hot at all.

Coaches decide *where* the leftover man comes from, too, not only how many. Inside-out settles the count; the
direction of the slide settles the side. Given the choice, they would rather leave the free rusher where the
quarterback can see him, on the side he is looking to throw, than coming from behind his back.

A [**sight adjust**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sight-adjust) is the receiver's half of the same idea. The
receiver sees the blitz too, and changes his route after the snap: a receiver running a deep route against a
defender who has just blitzed cuts it off short, stopping and turning back to the quarterback or breaking
inside, so the ball can come out immediately. The quarterback, reading the same blitz, expects it. Teams use
the two words differently. Some call any blitz-beater "hot," some reserve "hot" for a designated route and "sight"
for a converted one. What matters on the broadcast is the shape: a quick throw, often to a slot receiver or tight
end, into the space a blitzer just vacated.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden a "hot route" is something you do before the snap: you press a button and change one receiver's route
to a slant or a streak. Real offenses do change individual routes before the snap, with tags and signals, but
that is not what coaches mean by "hot." In football a hot route is the answer to an unblocked rusher: a throw
the quarterback makes *because* someone is coming free, to the space that rusher left. It is decided by the
defense's choice, after the snap, not by a menu.
:::

Hot throws explain a strange-looking fact you will start to notice: some of the most dangerous blitzes are the
ones that produce *quick completions*, not sacks. A six-man blitz that the offense has blocked correctly, inside-out,
leaves the quarterback a free rusher and a hot receiver. If he sees it, he completes a slant for eight yards;
if he doesn't, he is sacked from his blind side and the announcer blames the tackle, who did nothing wrong. Blitz
math, from the defense's side, is in [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd).

### The protection families, side by side

| Protection | Who blocks | Routes | An extra rusher is... | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Empty | 5 linemen (man, or a slide) | 5 | the QB's: throw hot | Empty sets, quick game |
| Scat | 5 linemen (back aligned in the backfield) | 5 | the QB's: throw hot | Quick throws |
| Half-slide | 5 linemen + back | 4, or 5 if the back releases | the back's (man side) or the slide's | Most ordinary dropbacks |
| Full slide | 5 linemen + back or TE | 4, or 5 if the back releases | the slide's; the back takes the end left behind | Stunts, inside pressure |
| Man (BOB) | 5 linemen + back | 4, or 5 if the back releases | the back's: the second linebacker | Clean four-man fronts |
| Seven-man | 5 linemen + back + TE | 3 on time, more late after check or chip | picked up; chips help the tackles | Long routes, a star edge rusher |
| Max protect | 7 or 8, all staying in | 2 or 3 | picked up by spare blockers | Deep shots, play-action |

: Pass protections by how many block and how many go out. Names and details vary by team; the counting does not. {tbl-colwidths="[13,24,17,27,19]"}

## The lineman's half: sets, punch and anchor

Schemes decide *who* blocks whom. Technique decides whether he can. Pass blocking is a strange athletic task:
a 315-pound man moving backward, against a man who is moving forward, faster and with a head start, who
knows where he is going. The offensive lineman's advantages are that he knows where the quarterback will be and
that he only has to stay in the way for about three seconds. Everything in his technique is built on those two
facts.

### The set: kick slide, vertical, 45-degree, jump

At the snap, a pass blocker **sets**: he rises out of his stance and moves to the spot from which he will meet his
rusher. For a tackle facing a fast edge rusher, the footwork is the
[**kick slide**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kick-slide). The outside foot kicks back and out, the inside foot
slides after it, and the feet never cross, so he can move backward and sideways while his shoulders stay square to
the line and he can still change direction. A tackle who crosses his feet, or turns his hips to run, has handed
the rusher the inside path to the quarterback.

Where the kick slide takes him is a choice, and the choice is a trade between time and space.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tackle-sets
#| fig-cap: "Three ways for a right tackle to set against a wide edge rusher (the dots are his footsteps). A vertical set kick-slides almost straight back for depth: the end must run a long arc around him. A 45-degree set goes back and out at an angle: he meets the rusher sooner, wider and with less ground given. A jump set attacks forward to meet the end at the line, taking away his running start; it pairs with quick throws, because if the tackle misses, the end has a short path to the quarterback."
SETS3 = [("Vertical set", (-3.7, 3.9), [(-1.4, 6.3), (-3.2, 5.0)],
          "Kick-slides straight back\nfor depth: the end must\ngo around him"),
         ("45-degree set", (-2.1, 4.7), [(-1.4, 5.9)],
          "Back and out at an\nangle: meets a wide\nrusher sooner"),
         ("Jump set", (-0.3, 4.5), [(0.2, 6.6), (-0.15, 5.4)],
          "Attacks at the line:\nno runway for the end;\nthe ball must come out fast")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
for ax, (name, rt_end, e_path, note) in zip(axes, SETS3):
    off = [q for q in line() if q.key in ("RG", "RT")]
    p = Play(off, [D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"), D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "E")], los=35, to_go=None)
    to(p, "RT", rt_end)
    to(p, "RE", e_path[-1], "rush", via=e_path[:-1])
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, title=False, lateral=(0.3, 8.0), window=(-5.2, 3.0))
    st, en = np.array([-0.7, 3.2]), np.array(rt_end)
    for i, f in enumerate(np.linspace(0.25, 0.85, 4)):      # footprints: kick (outside), slide (inside)
        q = st + (en - st) * f
        x, y = _P(fld, p, q[0], q[1] + (0.35 if i % 2 == 0 else -0.35))
        ax.plot([x], [y], marker="o", ms=3.0, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, alpha=0.6, zorder=5)
    panel_title(ax, name, size=8.4)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.02, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7.0, color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

A [**vertical set**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-vertical-set) kick-slides almost straight back, giving
ground fast. It is the answer to a speed rusher: the deeper the tackle gets, the longer the arc the rusher must run
around him, and the more likely the rusher ends up behind the quarterback. Its risk is the inside. A tackle who
has bailed straight back has left room between himself and his guard, and a good rusher will fake the arc and
come back underneath into that space.

A **45-degree set** goes back and out at an angle. It meets a wide rusher sooner and with less ground given, at the
cost of a little depth. Many tackles mix the two on purpose, so the rusher cannot time his moves to one picture.

A [**jump set**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jump-set) is the aggressive one: instead of retreating, the
blocker moves forward or flat to meet the rusher at or near the line of scrimmage. It takes away the rusher's
running start, the few yards he uses to build up speed before his move, and it gives the quarterback clean throwing
lanes on quick passes. It is also a gamble: a lineman who lunges and misses has nobody behind him, and the rusher's
path to the quarterback is now short. That is why jump sets travel with the quick game, when the ball will be gone
in a second and a half anyway, and why good tackles sprinkle them into longer dropbacks too, so rushers never
know what is coming.

Interior linemen set too, but differently: they have no room to give, so their sets are short, a step or two, and
their battles are decided almost immediately by hands and leverage.

### Punch and anchor

Once he has set, the blocker has to win the contact. The [**punch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punch) is his
weapon: a short, violent, two-handed strike into the rusher's chest, inside the rusher's arms, to stop his momentum
and take control of his body. Timing is everything. Punch too early and the rusher swats the hands away and runs
past; too late and the rusher's hands are already on the blocker's chest. That is why many NFL tackles no longer
throw one textbook two-handed punch against every rusher: against men who swipe and chop at the hands, they
"catch" the rusher and strike late, or use one hand at a time, so there is nothing early to swat. Hands *inside* matter for a second
reason: the rules. A blocker may first contact a rusher on or outside his frame (his body below the neck, facing
the blocker), but he must work immediately to get his hands inside it, and using hands or arms to grab, hook or
turn the rusher, restricting his path, is **holding**, wherever the hands are.[^holding] Hands outside the frame are
where a restriction is easiest to commit and easiest for an official to see. That is why linemen spend so much
