practice time on "inside hands": it is the safest place to win from.

The punch is only possible because of a rule change. Until 1978, pass blockers in the NFL had to keep their hands
close to their bodies; that season the league allowed them to extend their arms and open their hands, one of a
pair of rule changes meant to open up passing.[^1978] Before it, linemen pass-blocked with their forearms and
elbows, more like a wall of shoulders than a pair of arms. The change made the modern pass set, and the modern
passing game, possible. [The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) tells that story.

The [**anchor**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-anchor) is the answer to power. A [bull rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd)
(the rusher driving straight through the blocker's chest) does not try to get around the blocker; it tries to push
him backward into the quarterback. To anchor, the blocker drops his hips, widens his base and resets his feet so
that the push stops. A guard who cannot anchor is the most dangerous weakness a line can have, because the pocket
collapses from the middle, exactly where @fig-pocket-geometry said it must not.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Pass blocking is about strength." Strength matters most in the anchor, but most pass-blocking losses are losses of
*position* or *timing*: a set too shallow or too deep, a punch thrown too early, feet that stopped moving. That is
why some of the best pass-blocking tackles are not the strongest men on their line, and why a rusher's best moves,
the ones [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) describes, are aimed at the blocker's hands and feet,
not his strength.
:::

## Stunts: passing them off

The defense has its own way to beat protection without adding rushers: make two of them swap jobs. In a
[**stunt**](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) (also called a twist or a game), two rushers exchange gaps after the
snap. The most common is the [**T-E stunt**](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) (tackle first, end second): the
defensive tackle, here the 3-technique, goes first, crashing outward into the offensive tackle, and the end loops
around the back of him, on the defense's side of the line, into the space he left inside.
(Its mirror, the E-T stunt, sends the end inside first and loops the tackle around the outside.) The first man is
the **penetrator**; his job is to occupy, or even knock over, the blocker the looper needs to get past. The second is
the **looper**.

The offense's answer is the [**pass-off**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pass-off-switch-vs-stay): two adjacent
blockers handing the rushers to each other. There are two ways to do it, *switch* and *stay*, and the animation
shows the one coaches usually teach against a clean twist.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stunt-switch
#| fig-cap: "Passing off a T-E stunt by switching (simulated; the view is zoomed on the offense's right side, the quarterback is off the bottom of the frame, and the left side is blocked normally). The 3-technique (ringed in purple) slants hard outside into the right tackle while the end (ringed in green) jabs upfield and then loops around the back of him into the B gap. The right guard and right tackle stay on the same level and keep their areas: the tackle squeezes down and takes the 3-technique as he arrives, and the guard, instead of chasing the 3-technique outside, stays home and picks up the looping end. The dotted lines in the last frame show who finished on whom."
def stunt_play(switch=True):
    """A T-E stunt on the offense's right: the 3-technique crashes out into the tackle, the end loops inside
    behind him. switch=True: the RG and RT trade men. False: each follows the man he started on."""
    p = Play(line() + gun(None), four_down(lbs=False), los=35, to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.9, -7.4, 0.0)])
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.5, -0.6, -5.7), (1.0, -2.3, -5.6), (1.6, -3.3, -5.4)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.7, -4.0), (1.0, -2.8, -4.4), (1.6, -3.6, -4.3)], "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.5, 0.0, -0.9), (1.0, -0.5, -1.0), (1.6, -0.8, -1.0)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.5, -1.3, -1.6), (1.0, -1.7, -1.4), (1.6, -2.0, -1.3)], "block")
    timed(p, "C", [(0.5, -1.4, 0.1), (1.0, -1.8, 0.2), (1.6, -2.1, 0.3)], "block")
    # the penetrator: the 3-technique slants hard outside into the RT
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.4, 0.0, 3.0), (0.8, -0.7, 3.6), (1.1, -1.1, 3.9), (1.4, -1.35, 4.0), (1.8, -1.45, 4.0)], "rush")
    # the looper: the end jabs upfield, then loops around the back of the 3-technique (on the defense's side)
    loop = [(0.4, 0.1, 5.7), (0.8, 0.7, 4.7), (1.1, 0.5, 3.1), (1.4, -0.4, 2.2)]
    timed(p, "RE", loop + ([(1.8, -0.85, 2.0)] if switch else [(1.8, -2.2, 1.7), (2.2, -4.2, 1.1)]), "rush")
    if switch:
        # the RT squeezes down on the penetrator; the RG stays home and meets the looper
        timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.2, 1.9), (0.8, -1.6, 2.0), (1.1, -1.9, 2.0), (1.4, -2.1, 1.9), (1.8, -2.3, 1.9)], "block")
        timed(p, "RT", [(0.4, -1.4, 3.8), (0.8, -2.1, 4.0), (1.1, -2.5, 4.1), (1.4, -2.7, 4.1), (1.8, -2.85, 4.1)], "block")
    else:
        # stay: the RG chases the 3-technique outside; the RT, trying to follow the end inside, is cut off by them
        timed(p, "RG", [(0.4, -1.2, 2.1), (0.8, -1.8, 2.6), (1.1, -2.1, 2.9), (1.4, -2.3, 3.0), (1.8, -2.4, 3.0)], "block")
        timed(p, "RT", [(0.4, -1.6, 3.9), (0.8, -2.1, 4.4), (1.1, -2.5, 4.6), (1.4, -2.8, 4.6), (1.8, -2.9, 4.6)], "block")
    return p


protection_animation(stunt_play(True), [0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.1, 1.4, 1.8],
    notes=["snap: 3 over the RG,\nE over the RT", "3 crashes outside;\nE jabs upfield",
           "RT squeezes down on the 3;\nRG feels him leave", "E loops behind the 3;\nRG stays home",
           "switch: RT has the 3,\nRG meets the E", "two rushers, two blockers\n(dotted): nobody free"],
    lateral=(-1.2, 7.2), window=(-4.0, 2.4), ncols=3, rings=(("DT", PURPLE), ("RE", style.THIRD)),
    final_links=(("RT", "DT"), ("RG", "RE")))
```

**Switch** means each blocker keeps his *area* and takes whoever comes into it. In @fig-stunt-switch the guard
starts on the 3-technique, feels him crash outside, and lets him go to the tackle; the tackle starts on the end,
sees him loop away inside, and lets *him* go to the guard. Each lineman ends up on the other's man. The key coaching
point is that the two blockers must be **on the same level** (the same depth), "hip to hip." If the guard has set
deeper than the tackle, or shallower, the penetrator slips between them before the hand-off happens. Line coaches
add two cues: the tackle **squeezes** the penetrator, flattening down to meet him so he cannot split the seam, and
the guard gives him a push toward the tackle as he leaves and turns his eyes inside at once, because the looper is
coming next.

**Stay** means each blocker follows the man he started on, wherever he goes. Against a stunt, that usually loses,
and the static picture shows why.

```{python}
#| label: fig-stay-vs-switch
#| fig-cap: "The same T-E stunt, about two seconds after the snap, against two plans (simulated; faint lines are where each player has been). Left, stay: the right guard chases the 3-technique outside and the right tackle tries to chase the end inside, but the end's loop runs behind the guard and the 3-technique, and the tackle is cut off by his own teammate and the penetrator. Both blockers finish on the 3-technique, and the end is through the B gap toward the quarterback. Right, switch: each blocker kept his area, so each finished on the rusher who came into it."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
for ax, sw, ttl in zip(axes, (False, True), ("Stay: each chases his man", "Switch: each keeps his area")):
    q = stunt_play(sw)
    fld = panel(ax, q, tracking(q), 2.1, (-2.5, 7.5), (-8.8, 2.6), rings=(("DT", PURPLE), ("RE", style.THIRD)),
                links=() if not sw else (("RT", "DT"), ("RG", "RE")))
    panel_title(ax, ttl)
    if not sw:
        say(fld, q, -4.4, 4.9, "E is through\nthe B gap", color=RED, weight="bold")
        say(fld, q, 1.4, 5.6, "RG and RT both\nend up on the 3", color=RED, fontsize=6.8)
    else:
        say(fld, q, 1.4, 6.0, "RT took the 3,\nRG took the E", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)
plt.show()
```

The stunt is designed to beat "stay." The penetrator's crash outside drags the guard with him and puts two
bodies in the tackle's path, and the looper simply walks around the traffic. That is why most line coaches teach
switching against a clean two-man twist. Stay is not useless: if one blocker is already locked onto his man and
winning, letting go to switch can free the rusher he was beating, and some games are built to punish a switch,
with the looper waiting a beat (a delayed loop) so that the blockers trade too early. The decision is made in a
split second by feel, and it is a large part of why linemen who have played together for years protect better
than five talented strangers.

Notice, too, which scheme makes this easier. In a slide, every lineman already owns a gap, so a switch is the
default: the looper comes into the guard's gap, so he is the guard's. In man protection the blockers have to
recognise the stunt and *decide* to switch. That is one reason offenses facing stunt-heavy fronts lean on slide
protection. Where a stunt aims matters too. The T-E game in the figures attacks the guard-tackle seam; its mirror,
the E-T, sends the looper toward the guard-center seam, which is where a slide is strongest, because the center
and guards are all already stepping the same way. So defenses choose their games against the protection they
expect, and stunting is one of the main tools a four-man rush has for creating pressure without blitzing.

Linemen do talk through all of this. Before the snap they warn each other about alignments that suggest a stunt,
and during the rush a switch is often called out loud. On a broadcast you will almost never hear it; you see it in
the hand-off.

## The pocket over time

Everything so far has been about the first second or two. A real dropback lasts longer, and the pocket is not
a fixed shape; it breathes. It widens as the linemen set, holds for a while, and then shrinks as the rushers win
ground. Tracking data lets us draw that as a shape: join the five linemen and the quarterback with the smallest
polygon that contains them all (a *convex hull*), and you have a rough outline of the pocket, frame by frame.

The Big Data Bowl files this course uses ([13-05](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd))
record every player's position ten times a second. We have not downloaded those files, so the figure below uses
a *simulated* play from the `gridiron` library, written out in exactly the Big Data Bowl format; the code to run
the same measurement on a real play follows it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pocket-hull
#| fig-cap: "The pocket over time (simulated, BDB-format tracking; four-man rush against five blockers). The green shape is the convex hull of the five linemen and the quarterback. At the snap it is a thin triangle. By one second the linemen have set and the cup is at its widest. By two seconds the tackles are running the ends up their arcs, level with them, and the 1-technique's bull rush is driving the left guard back; the center, with nobody in his gap, has joined in to help. By three seconds the ends are at the quarterback's depth, the right end has come back underneath his tackle, and the quarterback has stepped up toward the right B gap, where the interior held, into a pocket shrinking from the front and closing from the side."
def pocket_play():
    """A four-man rush against five blockers, played out to 3.2 s: the edges are run up the arc, the 1-technique
    bull-rushes the left guard and the spare center helps, the right end beats his tackle late, and the
    quarterback steps up toward the right B gap."""
    p = Play(line() + gun(None), four_down(lbs=False), los=35, to_go=None)
    timed(p, "QB", [(0.9, -7.4, 0.0), (2.3, -7.4, 0.0), (2.8, -6.5, 0.8), (3.2, -6.4, 0.9)])
    timed(p, "LE", [(0.5, -0.6, -5.7), (1.0, -2.3, -5.6), (2.0, -4.6, -5.1), (3.0, -6.8, -3.7), (3.2, -7.1, -3.2)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LT", [(0.5, -1.7, -4.0), (1.0, -2.8, -4.4), (2.0, -4.3, -4.1), (3.0, -5.8, -2.8), (3.2, -6.1, -2.5)], "block")
    timed(p, "NT", [(0.5, 0.0, -0.9), (1.0, -0.6, -1.0), (2.0, -1.6, -1.0), (3.0, -2.4, -0.9), (3.2, -2.5, -0.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "LG", [(0.5, -1.3, -1.6), (1.0, -1.7, -1.3), (2.0, -2.7, -1.4), (3.0, -3.5, -1.4), (3.2, -3.6, -1.4)], "block")
    # the center: nobody in his gap, so he checks the middle and then posts onto the 1-technique's near hip
    timed(p, "C", [(0.5, -1.4, 0.2), (1.0, -1.8, 0.25), (2.0, -2.4, 0.15), (3.0, -3.1, 0.25), (3.2, -3.2, 0.25)], "block")
    timed(p, "DT", [(0.5, 0.0, 2.3), (1.0, -0.6, 2.2), (2.0, -1.0, 2.0), (3.0, -1.4, 1.9), (3.2, -1.5, 1.9)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RG", [(0.5, -1.3, 1.8), (1.0, -1.8, 1.9), (2.0, -2.2, 1.9), (3.0, -2.6, 1.9), (3.2, -2.7, 1.9)], "block")
    # the right end is run up the arc, then comes back underneath his tackle late
    timed(p, "RE", [(0.5, -0.6, 5.7), (1.0, -2.3, 5.6), (2.0, -4.6, 5.1), (2.6, -5.8, 4.4), (3.0, -6.2, 3.1), (3.2, -6.3, 2.6)], "rush")
    timed(p, "RT", [(0.5, -1.7, 4.0), (1.0, -2.8, 4.4), (2.0, -4.3, 4.1), (2.6, -5.3, 3.9), (3.0, -5.5, 4.0), (3.2, -5.5, 4.0)], "block")
    return p


pocket = pocket_play()
trk = pocket.to_tracking()          # simulated tracking in Big Data Bowl columns: frameId, time, x, y, ...
strip(pocket, [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0],
      notes=["snap: a straight wall\n(it becomes a cup)", "+1 s: sets made,\nthe cup at its widest",
             "+2 s: ends run up the arc;\nthe C helps the LG on the 1",
             "+3 s: the QB steps up;\nthe right end comes under"],
      lateral=(-7.5, 7.5), window=(-9.2, 2.6), ncols=2, hull=True)
plt.show()
```

The shape is useful because it can be turned into numbers, frame by frame, and the numbers tell the
story of the play without any video at all.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pocket-numbers
#| fig-cap: "The same simulated play as two measurements, one per tenth of a second. Left: the area of the pocket outline nearly doubles as the linemen set, then shrinks as the rush wins ground. Right: the distance from the quarterback to the nearest rusher, the space he has to throw in, stays near six yards for about two seconds and then falls fast. The dashed lines mark the frames shown above (1, 2 and 3 seconds)."
times = [t for t in sorted(trk["time"].unique()) if 0 <= t <= 3.2 + 1e-9]
area, space = [], []
for t in times:
    fr = trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], t)]
    area.append(hull_area(convex_hull(pocket_points(fr))))
    qb = fr.loc[fr["displayName"] == "QB", ["x", "y"]].to_numpy()[0]
    rushers = fr.loc[fr["side"] == "def", ["x", "y"]].to_numpy()
    space.append(float(np.min(np.hypot(*(rushers - qb).T))))
style.apply()
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.3))
ax1.plot(times, area, color=style.SERIES[2]); ax1.set_title("Pocket area (square yards)", fontsize=9)
ax2.plot(times, space, color=style.SERIES[1]); ax2.set_title("Quarterback to nearest rusher (yards)", fontsize=9)
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xlabel("seconds after the snap", fontsize=7.5)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 3.2)
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    for t in (1.0, 2.0, 3.0):
        ax.axvline(t, color=style.SERIES[6], lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On real data, the same two lines are a way to compare protections without trusting anyone's charting: how
quickly a team's pocket reaches its full size, how long it holds it, and how fast the quarterback's space
disappears. The code is the same; only the input changes.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the same measurement on a real Big Data Bowl play)"
# Run this after downloading a Big Data Bowl edition (see 13-05). Column names differ by year;
# gridiron.bdb.prepare() normalizes direction and labels each player 'off', 'def' or 'ball'.
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

trk_all = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_1.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
players = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/players.csv")[["nflId", "position"]]
one = bdb.prepare(trk_all, plays, game_id=2022091100, play_id=55)      # any dropback you choose
one = one.merge(players, on="nflId", how="left")
line_and_qb = one[one["position"].isin(["T", "G", "C", "QB"])]           # five linemen and the passer
for fid, fr in line_and_qb.groupby("frameId"):
    if fr["time"].iloc[0] < 0:
        continue
    print(fr["time"].iloc[0], hull_area(convex_hull(fr[["x", "y"]].to_numpy())))
```

## Measuring protection: pressure, time to throw and sacks

Now the numbers you will see on broadcasts and stat sites, and what each of them can and cannot tell you.

A **sack** (defined in [Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd))
is the number everyone knows: the quarterback tackled behind the line before he throws. Myles Garrett set the
single-season record with 23 of them in 2025.[^garrett] But sacks are rare (about six or seven per hundred
dropbacks) and they depend on many things besides the blocking, so analysts lean on broader measures.

[**Pressure**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure) is any rusher forcing the quarterback to change what he
wanted to do. It comes in three kinds: the sack; the [**QB hit**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-qb-hit-hurry),
contact that knocks the quarterback down or hits him as he throws; and the **hurry**, which forces him to throw
early or move off his spot without contact. [**Pressure rate**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pressure-rate) is
pressures divided by dropbacks. It is the
better measure of a protection (or a pass rush) because there are four or five pressures for every sack, so it
settles down faster and is less a matter of luck: whether a pressure becomes a sack depends a great deal on the
quarterback ([The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) looks at it from the defense's side).

There is one catch. **Pressure is a judgment, and different data providers judge it differently.** Some chart it
by eye from video; others use tracking data and a distance rule. The nflverse data this course uses carries a
pressure flag charted by FTN for recent seasons and by Next Gen Stats for earlier ones, and the two are not the
same series.[^pressure] (FTN is a football-data company whose staff chart every play from video; Next Gen Stats is the
league's own tracking-data service.) Compare pressure rates only within one source.

[**Time to throw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-time-to-throw) is the seconds from the snap to the release of
a pass, as measured by Next Gen Stats; their average leaves sacks out.[^ngs] It tells you how long a quarterback
holds the ball, which is partly the protection, partly the play call, and partly the quarterback.
Pressure rate and time to throw are tied together, and the
next chart shows how tightly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pressure-by-time
#| fig-cap: "The clock, in data: every pass thrown in the 2024 and 2025 regular seasons, grouped by time to throw. Left: the share of throws on which the quarterback was pressured climbs steadily, from under one in ten when the ball is out in two seconds to about three in four after five. Right: expected points added (EPA, the change in expected points a play produces, from 01-02) per throw rises at first, because longer-developing routes go deeper, peaks around three to three and a half seconds, and then falls off as pressure arrives. Sacks are left out of both panels, since a sack has no throw. Data: nflverse play-by-play and participation (FTN pressure charting) via nflreadpy."
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

style.apply()
FTN = [2024, 2025]
part = nfl().load_participation(seasons=FTN).to_pandas()[["nflverse_game_id", "play_id", "time_to_throw",
                                                           "was_pressure"]]
drop = pbp(FTN, columns=["game_id", "play_id", "season_type", "qb_dropback", "sack", "qb_hit", "epa"])
drop = drop[(drop["season_type"] == "REG") & (drop["qb_dropback"] == 1)].merge(
    part, left_on=["game_id", "play_id"], right_on=["nflverse_game_id", "play_id"], how="left")
press_rate = drop["was_pressure"].astype(float).mean()
press_to_sack = drop.loc[drop["was_pressure"] == True, "sack"].mean()   # noqa: E712
hit_rate = drop["qb_hit"].mean()
thrown = drop[drop["time_to_throw"].notna() & (drop["sack"] == 0)].copy()
EDGES = [0, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 5.0, 99]
LABS = ["<2.0", "2.0-2.5", "2.5-3.0", "3.0-3.5", "3.5-4.0", "4.0-5.0", "5.0+"]
thrown["bin"] = pd.cut(thrown["time_to_throw"], EDGES, labels=LABS, right=False)
byb = thrown.groupby("bin", observed=True).agg(n=("epa", "size"), epa=("epa", "mean"),
                                               pressure=("was_pressure", lambda s: s.astype(float).mean()))
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 2.9))
x = np.arange(len(LABS))
ax1.bar(x, 100 * byb["pressure"], color=style.SERIES[1], width=0.72)
ax1.set_title("Pressured (% of throws)", fontsize=9)
ax2.bar(x, byb["epa"], color=np.where(byb["epa"] >= 0, style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[7]), width=0.72)
ax2.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1)
ax2.set_title("EPA per throw", fontsize=9)
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.set_xticks(x, LABS, fontsize=7, rotation=35)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    ax.set_xlabel("time to throw (seconds)", fontsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-pressure-by-time as a picture of the bargain every pass play strikes. Across the two seasons, quarterbacks
were pressured on `{python} f"{100 * press_rate:.0f}%"` of dropbacks by FTN's charting, and about
`{python} f"{100 * press_to_sack:.0f}%"` of those pressures (roughly one in `{python} f"{1 / press_to_sack:.0f}"`)
ended in a sack; the play-by-play flags a quarterback hit on about `{python} f"{100 * hit_rate:.0f}%"` of
dropbacks. Throws out in under two seconds were pressured `{python} f"{100 * byb.loc['<2.0', 'pressure']:.0f}%"` of
the time; throws held past five seconds, `{python} f"{100 * byb.loc['5.0+', 'pressure']:.0f}%"`. The right panel
measures value in [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa), expected points added, from
[01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd): the change in the offense's expected points
from before the play to after it. The middle of the
range is where the offense profits: holding the ball three seconds buys deeper, more valuable throws, and the
protection's job is to make those three seconds safe. Past about three and a half, the rush is winning, and
value falls off a cliff. (These are averages over very different plays. A five-second throw is often a scramble or
a play that has broken down, which is part of why it does badly.)

**Sack rate** is sacks divided by dropbacks (pass attempts, sacks and scrambles). If protection were the whole
story, a team whose quarterback holds the ball longer would be sacked more, and by a lot. The next chart checks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ttt-sacks
#| fig-cap: "Holding the ball and getting sacked, team by team: every team-season from 2016 to 2025 (regular season). Time to throw is Next Gen Stats' average for the team's passers (snap to release, sacks excluded); sack rate is sacks per dropback from play-by-play. Teams that hold the ball longer are sacked a little more on average (the dashed trend), but the scatter around it is huge: at any given time to throw, sack rates range from about 3% to 10%. The arrow follows one team, the Chicago Bears, from 2024 to 2025. Data: nflverse via nflreadpy."
SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))
ngs = nfl().load_nextgen_stats(stat_type="passing", seasons=SEASONS).to_pandas()
ngs = ngs[(ngs["week"] > 0) & (ngs["season_type"] == "REG")].copy()
ngs["tw"] = ngs["avg_time_to_throw"] * ngs["attempts"]
ttt = ngs.groupby(["season", "team_abbr"]).agg(tw=("tw", "sum"), att=("attempts", "sum")).reset_index()
ttt["ttt"] = ttt["tw"] / ttt["att"]
plays = pbp(SEASONS, columns=["season", "season_type", "posteam", "qb_dropback", "sack"])
db = plays[(plays["season_type"] == "REG") & (plays["qb_dropback"] == 1)]
sk = db.groupby(["season", "posteam"]).agg(dropbacks=("sack", "size"), sacks=("sack", "sum")).reset_index()
sk["sack_rate"] = sk["sacks"] / sk["dropbacks"]
teams = ttt.merge(sk, left_on=["season", "team_abbr"], right_on=["season", "posteam"])
r_all = np.corrcoef(teams["ttt"], teams["sack_rate"])[0, 1]
r_25 = np.corrcoef(*teams.loc[teams["season"] == 2025, ["ttt", "sack_rate"]].to_numpy().T)[0, 1]
b = np.polyfit(teams["ttt"], 100 * teams["sack_rate"], 1)
league_ttt = teams.groupby("season").apply(lambda g: np.average(g["ttt"], weights=g["att"]), include_groups=False)
league_sr = db.groupby("season")["sack"].mean()
chi = teams[teams["posteam"] == "CHI"].set_index("season")
cin = teams[teams["posteam"] == "CIN"].set_index("season")
rank_25 = int(teams[teams["season"] == 2025].set_index("posteam")["ttt"].rank(ascending=False)["CHI"])
chi_ttt_rank = "the longest of any team that season" if rank_25 == 1 else f"the {rank_25}th-longest in the league"

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
old, new = teams[teams["season"] < 2025], teams[teams["season"] == 2025]
ax.scatter(old["ttt"], 100 * old["sack_rate"], s=16, color=style.GRID, edgecolor=style.MUTED, lw=0.4,
           label="2016-2024 team-seasons", zorder=2)
ax.scatter(new["ttt"], 100 * new["sack_rate"], s=30, color=style.SERIES[0], edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=1.0,
           label="2025", zorder=3)
xs = np.linspace(teams["ttt"].min(), teams["ttt"].max(), 10)
ax.plot(xs, np.polyval(b, xs), color=style.INK_2, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2, label="trend, all seasons")
a, z = chi.loc[2024], chi.loc[2025]
ax.annotate("", (z["ttt"], 100 * z["sack_rate"]), (a["ttt"], 100 * a["sack_rate"]),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.SERIES[1], lw=1.6, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=5), zorder=4)
ax.scatter([a["ttt"]], [100 * a["sack_rate"]], s=30, color=style.SERIES[1], edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=1.0,
           zorder=4, label="Bears 2024 (arrow: to 2025)")
ax.annotate(f"Bears 2024\n({a['sacks']:.0f} sacks)", (a["ttt"], 100 * a["sack_rate"]), xytext=(7, 4),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="left", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
ax.annotate(f"Bears 2025\n({z['sacks']:.0f} sacks)", (z["ttt"], 100 * z["sack_rate"]), xytext=(6, -12),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="left", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
ax.set_xlabel("Average time to throw (seconds, snap to release)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Sack rate (% of dropbacks)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three things to take from @fig-ttt-sacks.

**The ball is coming out a little later than it used to.** The league-wide average time to throw rose from
`{python} f"{league_ttt[2016]:.2f}"` seconds in 2016 to `{python} f"{league_ttt[2025]:.2f}"` in 2025, while the
league sack rate stayed within a point or so (`{python} f"{100 * league_sr[2016]:.1f}%"` of dropbacks in 2016,
`{python} f"{100 * league_sr[2025]:.1f}%"` in 2025). Quarterbacks hold the ball a fifth of a second longer than they
did a decade ago and are sacked only a little more often, which says something about how protection, and
quarterbacks' pocket movement, have kept up.

**Holding the ball explains only a little of who gets sacked.** Across all team-seasons the correlation between time
to throw and sack rate is `{python} f"{r_all:.2f}"`, positive but weak; the trend line says each extra tenth of a
second goes with about `{python} f"{b[0] / 10:.1f}"` more sacks per hundred dropbacks. Within 2025 alone it is
`{python} f"{r_25:.2f}"`, essentially nothing. Two teams can hold the ball equally long and be sacked at rates three
times apart. What separates them is the quality of the protection, the play calls, and above all the quarterback:
his sense of when to throw it away, when to step up, and when to run.

**Sacks are shared.** Follow the arrow. In 2024 the Bears' quarterback, Caleb Williams, was sacked
`{python} f"{chi.loc[2024, 'sacks']:.0f}"` times, a franchise record, on
`{python} f"{100 * chi.loc[2024, 'sack_rate']:.1f}%"` of dropbacks. In 2025, with a new head coach and three new
interior linemen, he was sacked `{python} f"{chi.loc[2025, 'sacks']:.0f}"` times
(`{python} f"{100 * chi.loc[2025, 'sack_rate']:.1f}%"`) *while holding the ball longer*:
`{python} f"{chi.loc[2025, 'ttt']:.2f}"` seconds on average, `{python} chi_ttt_rank`, up from
`{python} f"{chi.loc[2024, 'ttt']:.2f}"`.[^bears] The new linemen were the guards Joe Thuney (traded from Kansas
City) and Jonah Jackson (from the Rams) and the center Drew Dalman (signed in free agency), all in the interior, the
part of the pocket @fig-pocket-geometry said must never give ground. Same quarterback, more time, a third as many
sacks. Some of that is the line, some the scheme (Ben Johnson was the new head coach), some a second-year
quarterback learning when to get rid of the ball. The data cannot split the credit, and neither can anyone who
blames every sack on the left tackle. If you rewatch a 2025 Bears dropback next to a 2024 one, watch the interior:
do the guards and center hold their ground, so that Williams can step up and throw, or step up and run?

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Sacks allowed measures the offensive line." It measures the whole passing operation. A quarterback who holds the
ball waiting for a deep route, refuses to throw it away, or drifts into the rush creates sacks no line could
prevent, and a quarterback with a quick trigger hides a weak one. Analysts who want to grade the line alone use
measures built from individual matchups, such as pass-block win rate or charted pressures allowed per blocker,
and even those are noisy. When you hear "the line gave up five sacks," ask how many of them came after three
seconds.
:::

## Where protection came from

Pass protection as a *system*, with named schemes, counted assignments and a back with a rule, is younger than
you might think, and two moments explain most of its shape.

The first is the 1978 rule change you met above. Before it, linemen could not extend their arms on a pass block, so
protection was a matter of bodies in the way: a pass rusher who got his hands on a lineman had most of the
advantages, and passing on long downs was dangerous. Letting blockers use their hands, together with new limits
on how defenders could contact receivers, tilted the game toward the pass for good.[^1978-2]

The second is a player. Lawrence Taylor, the New York Giants' outside linebacker from 1981, rushed the passer from
a standing position off the edge, faster than any tackle could handle alone, and from a spot that standard
protections assigned to a running back. Offenses had to invent ways to put a bigger man on him. Joe Gibbs, whose
Washington teams played the Giants twice a year, is credited with building his one-back, two-tight-end
formations partly to do exactly that: an extra tight end or an "H-back" lined up beside the tackle to block or chip
Taylor, so that the back was never left alone with him.[^lt] The chip, the help side and the seven-man protection,
and the idea that the left tackle protecting a right-handed quarterback's [blind side](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd)
is a premium position, all
trace back to offenses deciding that one great rusher had to be accounted for before anyone else.

Since then the arms race has run in both directions. Defenses answered slide protections with stunts and with
pressure that showed six and rushed four; offenses answered blitzes with hot routes and the quick game, and
with quarterbacks and centers who could reset a protection at the line. The Mike call you hear on every broadcast
is the current front of that race.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cincinnati Bengals 2022 — rebuilding a line, and three backups in Buffalo"}
**The problem.** In 2021 Joe Burrow was sacked a league-high 51 times in the regular season and another 19 times in
the playoffs, including nine in the divisional round against Tennessee and seven by the Rams in Super Bowl LVI,
which tied the Super Bowl record.[^bengals21] The Bengals went to the Super Bowl anyway, and lost it with their
quarterback on the ground.

**The rebuild.** That offseason Cincinnati signed center Ted Karras, guard Alex Cappa and tackle La'el Collins,
and drafted guard Cordell Volson: four new starters around Burrow.[^bengals22] The team's sack rate fell from
`{python} f"{100 * cin.loc[2021, 'sack_rate']:.1f}%"` of dropbacks in 2021 to
`{python} f"{100 * cin.loc[2022, 'sack_rate']:.1f}%"` in 2022.

**The test.** By the 2022 playoffs, injuries had taken three of the five starters, and in the divisional round at
Buffalo on January 22, 2023, the Bengals started three backups: Jackson Carman, a second-year player whose six
previous starts had all come at right guard, at left tackle; Max Scharping at right guard; and Hakeem Adeniji at
right tackle. They won 27–10 and Burrow was sacked once and
hit only three times.[^buffalo] It is a good game to rewatch with this chapter's tools: look for help on the backup
tackles from tight ends and backs, and for how quickly the ball comes out.

**The limit.** A week later, in the AFC Championship Game at Kansas City (January 29, 2023), the same patched line
gave up five sacks, two of them by defensive tackle Chris Jones, the second on third down on Cincinnati's last
possession, which forced the punt before the Chiefs' winning drive; rookie end George Karlaftis had the first, on the
game's fifth play. Kansas City won 23–20.[^kc] Schemes can hide a
weak spot for a while. A great rusher, given enough snaps, finds it.

**What to notice:** on a Bengals rewatch, count blockers on third down, in a game with the healthy line and in one
with the backups, and see whether the offense kept more men in to protect the patched line.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Philadelphia Eagles 2013–2025 — the Stoutland line"}
Jeff Stoutland coached the Eagles' offensive line from 2013 through the 2025 season, a run that included both of the
franchise's Super Bowl titles (LII and LIX), and he was regarded as one of the best offensive line coaches in the
league.[^stoutland] His lines were known for athletic, technically precise linemen (Lane Johnson at right tackle, Jason
Kelce and then Cam Jurgens at center, Jordan Mailata at left tackle) and, in Kelce's years, for a center who made most
of the protection calls; after Kelce retired, Jurgens and quarterback Jalen Hurts shared that job.[^eaglescalls]
The Eagles are also a reminder that a great line and a great run game go together: the same men who pass protect
also block for the backs and for the [tush push](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).
[Case study 12-06](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd) goes deeper.

**What to notice:** on any Eagles dropback, watch Lane Johnson's first two steps. You will see vertical sets,
45-degree sets and, on quick throws, a jump set right at the line, varied so the rusher cannot time his move.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**Before the snap.**

- **Count the blockers you can see.** Five linemen, plus a back beside the quarterback, plus any tight end on the
  line. Empty backfield means five-man protection: someone is hot.
- **Count the threats.** How many defenders are standing within a couple of yards of the line? Six or seven at the
  line against five or six blockers means a hot throw is in the plan, or the defense is bluffing.
- **Listen and look for the Mike call.** The center or quarterback points at a linebacker. If a defender moves
  after that, watch for a second call.
- **Find the help.** A tight end next to a tackle may mean that side's edge rusher is getting a chip. A back offset
  to one side more often shows his *check* side, the side he will watch for a blitzer (usually the man side, away
  from the slide), and maybe chip after. Neither is a guarantee: a late call can send him across the
  quarterback's face.

**After the snap: rushers versus blockers.**

- **Watch the linemen's first step.** All five the same way: slide. The center and his two neighbours one way,
  the other two straight back at the man in front of them: half-slide. Each to a different defender: man.
- **Count, in the first second, how many rushed and how many blocked.** Four rushers against six blockers? Look
  for the spare men helping. Six against six? Everyone has a man.
- **Watch the back's first step.** Forward into a gap: he has a blitzer. Out to the flat: his man dropped
  (check-release). A shove on an end and then out: a chip.
- **Watch the tackles' sets.** Deep and backward (vertical), angled out (45-degree), or forward at the line (jump,
  and expect a quick throw).
- **If a rusher comes free, guess who owned him.** Was he the widest man, unblocked on purpose, with the ball out
  fast to the space he left? That was the plan. Was he an inside man, a linebacker through an A gap, with two blockers
  on someone else? That was a bust, probably a bad count. Check the replay. And look at the ball: a free man by
  design should be met by a quick throw. If the widest man came free and the ball was *not* out, the quarterback
  or the hot receiver missed it; if an inside man came free, suspect the protection first.
- **Note the time.** Count "one-Mississippi" from the snap. Pressure inside about two and a half seconds is
  almost always the protection's problem: the average throw is out by then. Past three seconds, where the EPA chart
  above peaked and started to fall, the quarterback owns part of it. These are rules of thumb from that chart, not
  laws.

**For your prediction log:** for one quarter, write down rushers and blockers on every dropback (for example,
"4 v 6") and whether anyone came free. By the end you will know whether that defense wins by numbers or by stunts.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: seven at the line"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-empty
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-7. The offense is in an empty 3x2 formation: five blockers. The defense has two 3-techniques, shows both linebackers standing in the A gaps on either side of the center, and has walked the nickel back (NB) up over H. The three defenders who might or might not rush are ringed."
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -2.4, "3"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.8, 0.95, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.8, -0.95, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 2.0, -7.6, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.0, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.0, 14.0, "C"),
       D("SS", "SS", 6.5, 10.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(empty_3x2(), dfn, los=40, to_go=7)
p.highlight("MIKE", "WILL", "NB", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-6.8, 14.6), ol_fs=6.2)
plt.show()
```

**How many can the offense block, how many might come, and where should the ball go if they all do?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Five blockers, up to seven rushers, so the ball must come out fast, with a hot answer on each side.** Count it:
four defensive linemen, two linebackers in the A gaps and the walked-up nickel make seven possible rushers against
an empty protection's five. If all seven come, two are free; there is no protection that blocks seven with five.

*Which* two is the offense's choice. Inside-out, the five linemen take the two A-gap linebackers and the two
3-techniques first, because their paths are shortest, and the fifth blocker goes to one of the ends. The offense
picks the end by working the protection toward the side with more threats. The left has four possible rushers (the
Will, a 3-technique, the end and the nickel), the right only three, so the line works left and the left tackle takes
the left end. The two men left over are then the widest on each side: the nickel on the left and the right end on
the right, each with the longest way to go.

Two free rushers need two answers. On the left, H is hot: if the nickel comes, H runs into the space he left. On the
right, count the *coverage* as well as the rush, which is the first thing a quarterback coach asks. If seven rush,
only four defenders are left to cover five receivers, so someone is uncovered; as drawn, nobody is over R. The
quarterback's throw depends on who actually comes, and it has to be out in about a second.

Two cautions. First, this is exactly the look that attacks the Mike call: with two linebackers in the A gaps, the
offense must decide before the snap which one the line will count, and the defense will try to make him wrong.
Second, the defense may not bring them all. Showing seven and rushing four, with the A-gap linebackers dropping out,
is a staple of [simulated pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd). Then the hot throw is
thrown into a linebacker who never left. Good quarterbacks check where the threat goes at the snap, not where it
stood.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: two on the edge"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-edge
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6. The offense is in 11 personnel with the back to the quarterback's left and has called a half-slide right (the slide side's gaps are shaded), so the back's job is the left side. The Will linebacker has walked up to the line outside the left end, and the nickel back has crept down outside him, both ringed. The back is ringed in green."
off = line() + gun(-1.5) + [O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, -8.5), O("Y", "TE", -1.4, 8.5),
                            O("Z", "WR", -0.7, 13.5)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.4, -6.6, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.9, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.5, "C"),
       D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.5, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=6)
p.highlight("WILL", "NB", color=PURPLE)
p.highlight("RB")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-6.8, 14.6), ol_fs=6.2)
for wg in (0.8, 2.4, 4.0):
    gap_oval(fld, p, wg, width=1.4, height=1.2, alpha=0.42)
say(fld, p, -3.2, 6.2, "slide right", color=GREEN, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

**(a) If both the Will and the nickel blitz from the left, whom does the back block, and who is the quarterback's
problem?**

**(b) Now a post-snap read.** Suppose that instead the Mike comes through the right A gap untouched, while the
center has turned left to help the left guard on the 1-technique. Was the Mike free by design, or was it a bust? And
whose was he?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**(a) The back takes the Will; the nickel is the quarterback's, and the throw goes to H.** On the left, the man side,
the left tackle has the end and the left guard has the 1-technique. That leaves two potential rushers, the Will and the
nickel, and one back. Block inside-out: the Will is closer to the quarterback's path, so he is the back's; the
nickel, wider and deeper, has the longer way to go and is left free by design. His blitz empties the area over H, so H
is the hot receiver, and the quarterback has to see the nickel come and throw at once.

The offense had other options before the snap: the quarterback could have re-declared the protection, sliding the
line left toward the threat and sending the back right, or kept the tight end in. Notice why it might not bother:
the right side has only three rushers for three sliding linemen, and a quick throw to H against a blitzing nickel is
often the best play on the field. If the nickel *doesn't* come, the back's man (the Will) still might, and if neither
comes, the back releases and five receivers are out.

**(b) A bust, and the Mike was the center's.** In a half-slide right, the center owns the right A gap, whoever
comes through it. He may "look for work" and help a neighbour only once nobody has come into his gap; turning left
first left his own gap empty. Every tell in the "Watch for it" list points the same way: the free man came from
the inside, through an A gap, the shortest path, while two blockers were on one defender. A free man by design is the
widest man, and the ball is already on its way to the space he left.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the star on the edge"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-star
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-10. The defense's best pass rusher (99, ringed) lines up wide outside the offense's right tight end. The offense has the tight end on the line next to the right tackle and the back offset to the right of the quarterback, with two receivers to the left."
off = line() + gun(1.6) + [O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.5), O("H", "WR", -1.4, -8.5),
                           O("Z", "WR", -1.4, 13.0)]
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), D("NT", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT", "DT", 1.0, 2.35, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 7.2, "99"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.1, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -13.5, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 13.0, "C"),
       D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 8.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
p.highlight("RE", color=PURPLE)
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.4, lateral=(-15.6, 15.6), window=(-6.8, 14.6), ol_fs=6.2)
point_to(fld, p, (4.6, 10.0), (1.0, 7.2), "their best pass rusher,\nwide outside the tight end")
plt.show()
```

**Where is the protection's help going, and what does the offense give up to send it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**99 belongs to the right tackle, and the help comes on top: chips from the tight end and the back. The price is
receivers and time.** Everything about the offense's alignment points at the right edge. Expect a half-slide
*left*: the center, left guard and left tackle slide left and own the gaps on that side (the 1-technique, the Will
and the left end), while on the man side the right guard takes the 3-technique and the right tackle takes 99 man to
man, big on big. Then the help. The tight end chips 99 from the inside as he releases. The back, offset to that side,
checks his linebacker (the Mike) first; if the Mike doesn't come, he chips 99 too and releases (check, chip,
release). If the offense wants a full-time double team instead, it is the tackle and the tight end together, a
seven-man protection.

What the offense will not do is leave 99 to the tight end and the back. You never leave a star alone with a back;
help means *in addition to* the tackle.

The cost is visible too. With two players spending time on 99, only three receivers (X, H and Z) are out on time, and
the tight end and back arrive late, so expect a throw to the receivers who are on time, or a two- or three-man
route combination with lots of protection behind it. The defense's answer is just as predictable: move 99 around (inside, to the
other side, standing up over a guard) or run stunts with him, so that the offense's help is in the wrong place.
That cat-and-mouse is where [The Pass Rush](../07-pressure/07-01-pass-rush.qmd) picks up the story.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Protection is counting.** The offense always blocks with five and may add a back or tight ends; every added
  blocker is one fewer receiver. Block inside-out, and if someone must go unblocked, make it the widest man and
  make him the quarterback's.
- **Two ways to assign blockers.** Slide protection blocks gaps, so it absorbs stunts and surprises but leaves an
  end for the back. Man protection (BOB) blocks men, so it matches big on big but has to chase movement. The
  half-slide, the everyday six-man protection, does both. Slide toward the inside trouble, and never leave a star
  edge rusher alone with a back.
- **The Mike call makes six blockers one mind.** Naming a reference defender sets every assignment (the center
  works toward him, the man side counts out from him, the back takes the next man); two blockers
  counting from different men produce a free rusher without the defense sending an extra man. Defenses move after
  the call to make it wrong.
- **Backs and tight ends decide after the snap.** Check-release turns a blocker into a receiver when his man
  doesn't come; a chip gives help on the way out. Max protect buys time with up to eight blockers; empty and scat
  buy receivers with five, and a blitz means a hot throw or a sight adjust into the space the blitzer left.
- **The pocket is a cup.** The interior holds firm; the tackles give ground with a kick slide (vertical, 45-degree,
  or a jump set for quick throws) and push the edge past the quarterback, who steps up. Punch wins control, the
  anchor stops power, and switching beats stunts.
- **Measure pressure, not just sacks, and share the blame.** Pressure rate is steadier than sack rate; pressure
  climbs with time to throw; and sack rate depends on the quarterback and the play call as much as on the line.
